deduped_items.title: Poutine prêt à fournir du pétrole aux Etats-Unis, Zelensky réagit
deduped_items.summary: Le président russe Vladimir Poutine a affirmé vendredi à son homologue Donald Trump que la Russie était disposée à "fournir du pétrole aux marchés américain et mondial" dans un contexte de crise du carburant. Ce projet, confirmé par M. Trump, a suscité de sévères critiques du président ukrainien Volodymyr Zelensky, qui a dénoncé une décision "indigne" et "faible" de la part de Washington, au moment où une délégation ukrainienne se trouve aux Etats-Unis pour négocier.

deduped_items.title: A l’aube de l’élection présidentielle, une envie de renverser le « système » traverse la jeunesse française
deduped_items.summary: D’un côté, le climat, les questions de genre et d’inclusion, l’effroi de voir l’extrême droite arriver au pouvoir… De l’autre, des peurs identitaires, le sentiment de voir la France s’affaiblir et disparaître dans le magma mondial… Deux jeunesses se retrouvent dos à dos avec l’envie d’une rupture radicale en 2027, analyse Matthieu Goar, l’un des chefs du service Politique du « Monde ».

deduped_items.title: Abbas postpones Palestinian elections, sets presidential poll for September 2027
deduped_items.summary: RAMALLAH, Oct 10 - Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday cancelled legislative elections scheduled for November due to worsening conditions within the Palestinian territories and set a date of September 11, 2027 for both presidential and legislative elections, the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.
deduped_items.body_text:
Abbas postpones Palestinian elections, sets presidential poll for September 2027
RAMALLAH, Oct 10 - Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday cancelled legislative elections scheduled for November due to worsening conditions within the Palestinian territories and set a date of September 11, 2027 for both presidential and legislative elections, the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.
Abbas' decree cited "obstacles posed by Israeli measures" to holding elections in November and the need to establish suitable political, security and on-the-ground conditions for "free, fair and inclusive elections". It called on Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza to participate in the polls.
There had been serious doubts that the Palestinian Authority vote would go ahead in late November. The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-06, after which Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas' rival, the Islamist group Hamas, seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists.
The decree said Israeli military attacks, settlement expansion, settler violence and movement restrictions in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, along with Israel's continued withholding of Palestinian tax revenues, created challenges to preparing for and holding elections on the previous date.
In Gaza, the decree pointed to "exceptional security and humanitarian conditions", the incomplete withdrawal of Israeli forces, the lack of progress in reconstruction and the failure to implement arrangements for deploying international stabilisation forces and police.
Israeli restrictions on access for election commission staff and international observers to Gaza and East Jerusalem also complicated preparations, the decree said.
The decision to postpone followed a resolution by the Palestine Liberation Organisation's executive committee and consultations with Palestinian factions and political forces. It also aimed to allow time for a comprehensive Palestinian national dialogue to strengthen unity and address challenges facing the electoral process. REUTERS

deduped_items.title: Abbas postpones Palestinian elections, sets presidential poll for September 2027
deduped_items.summary: RAMALLAH, Oct 10 - Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday cancelled legislative elections scheduled for November due to worsening conditions within the Palestinian territories and set a date of September 11, 2027 for both presidential and legislative elections, the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.
deduped_items.body_text:
Abbas postpones Palestinian elections, sets presidential poll for September 2027
RAMALLAH, Oct 10 - Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday cancelled legislative elections scheduled for November due to worsening conditions within the Palestinian territories and set a date of September 11, 2027 for both presidential and legislative elections, the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.
Abbas' decree cited "obstacles posed by Israeli measures" to holding elections in November and the need to establish suitable political, security and on-the-ground conditions for "free, fair and inclusive elections". It called on Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza to participate in the polls.
There had been serious doubts that the Palestinian Authority vote would go ahead in late November. The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-06, after which Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas' rival, the Islamist group Hamas, seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists.
The decree said Israeli military attacks, settlement expansion, settler violence and movement restrictions in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, along with Israel's continued withholding of Palestinian tax revenues, created challenges to preparing for and holding elections on the previous date.
In Gaza, the decree pointed to "exceptional security and humanitarian conditions", the incomplete withdrawal of Israeli forces, the lack of progress in reconstruction and the failure to implement arrangements for deploying international stabilisation forces and police.
Israeli restrictions on access for election commission staff and international observers to Gaza and East Jerusalem also complicated preparations, the decree said.
The decision to postpone followed a resolution by the Palestine Liberation Organisation's executive committee and consultations with Palestinian factions and political forces. It also aimed to allow time for a comprehensive Palestinian national dialogue to strengthen unity and address challenges facing the electoral process. REUTERS

deduped_items.title: Meloni’s overhaul of Italian electoral system | Explained
deduped_items.summary: The new rules, approved by lawmakers in a secret ballot with 227 votes against 164, scraps the first-past-the-post seats and puts the whole parliament under proportional representation. deduped_items.summary: In 1998, Michael Jordan laced up a pair of his iconic black and red Air Jordan 13s to bring home a Bulls victory during Game 2 of his final NBA championship — and now they are the most expensive sneakers ever to sell at auction. The game-winning sneakers sold for $2.2 million at Sotheby's in New York on Tuesday, smashing the sneaker auction record of $1.47 million, set in 2021 by a pair of Nike Air Ships that Jordan wore earlier in his career.

deduped_items.title: Massive 7.7 magnitude earthquake strikes Panama as officials investigate potential tsunami threat
deduped_items.summary: A powerful earthquake struck Panama's southern coast Friday, prompting officials to investigate a possible tsunami threat after the USGS lowered its magnitude estimate from 8.0 to 7.7.
deduped_items.body_text:
A powerful 7.7 magnitude earthquake struck off Panama's southern coast Friday, shaking the country's capital as officials investigated a potential tsunami threat.
The U.S. Geological Survey initially measured the earthquake at magnitude 8.0 before lowering its estimate to 7.7. The quake struck at 1:56 p.m. ET, at a depth of 7.8 miles, near Pitaloza Arriba, Panama.
A 5.5 magnitude aftershock followed, with its epicenter approximately 50 miles east of the initial earthquake.
The Panama Canal said operations were continuing normally following Friday's earthquake, with emergency protocols activated and technical teams inspecting facilities for possible damage. Canal officials said their priority was ensuring the safety of workers, vessels, crews and nearby communities as assessments continued.
The earthquake was felt in Panama City and in San José, the capital of neighboring Costa Rica, according to Reuters.
Tsunami officials warned that waves reaching 3 to 10 feet above tide levels were possible along some coastal areas of Panama, while parts of Ecuador could experience waves of approximately 1 to 3 feet.
Smaller tsunami waves of less than 1 foot above tide levels were forecast for coastal areas of Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Mexico, Nicaragua and Peru.
COLOMBIA BUILDING COLLAPSES ON CAMERA AS EARTHQUAKE BRINGS DEATH, DESTRUCTION
Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino said in a series of posts on X that he was visiting areas affected by Friday's earthquake and coordinating emergency assistance with government officials.
Mulino said he had ordered the mobilization of personnel, resources and aid for affected communities, along with structural assessments to determine the extent of the damage. He also thanked neighboring countries for their support and said assistance from the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean (CAF) would go toward helping those affected.
The president said he was traveling through Penonomé with government officials to coordinate relief efforts and thanked the United States and other countries for their offers of assistance.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a Friday post on X that the State Department was rapidly mobilizing resources and personnel to assist Panama at the request of the Panamanian government. Rubio said the U.S. was closely monitoring the earthquake and directed Americans needing assistance to the department's 24-hour consular hotline at +1-202-501-4444 from abroad or +1-888-407-4747 from the U.S. and Canada.
The U.S. Embassy in Panama also said it was assessing potential damage and working to account for the safety and whereabouts of visitors and personnel. In a separate X post, the embassy urged Americans in Panama to enroll in the State Department's Smart Traveler Enrollment Program at STEP.State.gov and follow its social media accounts for updates.
Despite the potential danger to coastal communities near the earthquake, officials said a Pacific-wide tsunami was not expected.
Earthquakes measuring between 7.0 and 7.9 can cause serious damage, according to Michigan Technological University.

Information about possible damage or casualties from Friday's earthquake was not immediately available.

A powerful 7.7 magnitude earthquake struck off Panama's southern coast Friday, shaking the country's capital as officials investigated a potential tsunami threat.
The U.S. Geological Survey initially measured the earthquake at magnitude 8.0 before lowering its estimate to 7.7. The quake struck at 1:56 p.m. ET, at a depth of 7.8 miles, near Pitaloza Arriba, Panama.
A 5.5 magnitude aftershock followed, with its epicenter approximately 50 miles east of the initial earthquake.
The Panama Canal said operations were continuing normally following Friday's earthquake, with emergency protocols activated and technical teams inspecting facilities for possible damage. Canal officials said their priority was ensuring the safety of workers, vessels, crews and nearby communities as assessments continued.
The earthquake was felt in Panama City and in San José, the capital of neighboring Costa Rica, according to Reuters.
Tsunami officials warned that waves reaching 3 to 10 feet above tide levels were possible along some coastal areas of Panama, while parts of Ecuador could experience waves of approximately 1 to 3 feet.
Smaller tsunami waves of less than 1 foot above tide levels were forecast for coastal areas of Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Mexico, Nicaragua and Peru.

deduped_items.title: US Army Corps of Engineers failed to explain drop in environmental mitigation work: Watchdog
deduped_items.summary: A chart published by GAO shows a sharp decline in the agency's decisions to make mitigation plans for wildlife and habitat protection from 2022 to 2025.
deduped_items.body_text:
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers did not seek to mitigate environmental damage for more than 50 projects over the past five years and did not provide detailed explanations to Congress, a government watchdog found.
Measures to prevent environmental damage were proposed in only 22 of 74 civil works projects the Corps submitted to Congress for approval from 2020 to 2025, according to a report published Wednesday by the Government Accountability Office.
The Corps deemed that no such measures were needed for the remaining 52 projects and failed to provide detailed evidence as to why, the watchdog alleges.
The agency regularly works to improve water navigation channels to prevent flooding and restore aquatic habitats around the country through its civil works program. It is required by statute to make detailed reports to Congress outlining whether its projects will require measures to prevent possible harm to fish, wildlife and the environment.
The engineers are expected “to plan for environmental mitigation — that is, to take actions to avoid, minimize, or compensate for expected losses to fish and wildlife and damage to ecological resources,” which could include reinforcing riverbanks or restoring wetland areas to create new habitats for fish and wildlife, according to the report.
The Corps of Engineers may decide not to undertake conservation measures if it deems certain projects will not cause harm. However, the Army is expected to provide Congress with clear explanations for those decisions.
A chart published by GAO shows a sharp decline in the Corps’ decisions to make mitigation plans for wildlife and habitat protection from 2022 to 2025. In 2024, for example, the agency decided that only one of 13 projects would require measures to safeguard the environment.
The GAO’s chart shows zero mitigation plans made in 2025.
In its findings, the GAO alleges that the Corps failed to provide necessary details to Congress demonstrating the reasons behind its decision-making in cases when it deemed no environmental protection measures were needed.
The watchdog said the vast majority of documents sent to Congress during those five years contained broad and general language that failed to clarify how the Corps reached its decisions.
The GAO recommended that the Army establish clear guidance for the Corps to document how it reaches decisions to keep Congress and the public better informed.
The Army disputed the GAO’s recommendations in a Sept. 16 letter signed by D. Lee Forsgren, the senior official performing the duties of the Army’s assistant secretary for civil works.
“We do not concur with the recommendation in the draft that we need to create more guidance about mitigation decision making on Civil Works projects,” Forsgren wrote.
“The water resources project reports (including associated Chief’s Reports) produced by USACE have sufficient technical information for decision makers and the public and resource agencies to understand when habitat mitigation is or is not included in a final recommendation.”
Zita Ballinger Fletcher previously served as editor of Military History Quarterly and Vietnam magazines and as the historian of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration. She holds an M.A. with distinction in military history.

The engineers are expected “to plan for environmental mitigation — that is, to take actions to avoid, minimize, or compensate for expected losses to fish and wildlife and damage to ecological resources,” which could include reinforcing riverbanks or restoring wetland areas to create new habitats for fish and wildlife, according to the report.

A chart published by GAO shows a sharp decline in the Corps’ decisions to make mitigation plans for wildlife and habitat protection from 2022 to 2025. In 2024, for example, the agency decided that only one of 13 projects would require measures to safeguard the environment.

“We do not concur with the recommendation in the draft that we need to create more guidance about mitigation decision making on Civil Works projects,” Forsgren wrote.
“The water resources project reports (including associated Chief’s Reports) produced by USACE have sufficient technical information for decision makers and the public and resource agencies to understand when habitat mitigation is or is not included in a final recommendation.”

Join War on the Rocks and gain access to content trusted by policymakers, military leaders, and strategic thinkers worldwide.
                            Lucas Ziller                        
October 9, 2026
A kill chain measured in seconds cannot depend on processes measured in weeks or months. The Pentagon recognizes that drone proliferation and AI-enabled lethal targeting are reducing decision cycles and increasing the premium on speed. The 2025 drone and acquisition reforms and the 2026 Artificial Intelligence Strategy call for faster procurement, fewer integration barriers, open architectures, continuous experimentation, and greater access to emerging technology.
Yet the experience of myself and fellow soldiers in the 1st Brigade Combat Team, 82nd Airborne Division (1/82), before and during its deployment in support of Operation Epic Fury shows that this reform agenda falls short at the tactical edge. For all the progress made in the Pentagon and combatant commands to speed up the kill chain, those at the very tip of the spear still face delays in integrating drones, targeting software, networks, and fires systems. Policies designed to accelerate innovation have not consistently given brigade-level formations the authorities, technical support, and development access needed to assemble and adapt integrated kill chains during operations. The Army has the technology to compete, but institutional latency constrains tactical formations’ ability to adapt.
Tactical commanders need the authority, access, and technical support to control and adapt their own kill chains, while maintaining targeting authorities and human judgment over the use of force. Closing this gap requires delegating purchasing authority to brigade commanders, delegating integration authority to division commanders, providing dedicated technical support to brigades, and giving tactical formations direct access to AI development.
A kill chain is the process of detecting and confirming an enemy target, transmitting the information to a shooter, engaging the target, and assessing the effects. A fully digital kill chain would network sensors and shooters within a shared computing environment, enabling AI to rapidly recognize targets and autonomously pair them to appropriate firing systems, while keeping trained operators responsible for lethal decisions. This ideal is still far from the reality experienced by soldiers today.
For example, 1/82’s legacy kill chain process involved a sensor, such as a drone, using full-motion video to observe possible targets. Junior paratroopers, with limited training and less than a year of experience in drone-enabled kill chains, watched the video, wrote down the grids in their notebooks, and verbally transmitted them as a separate fire mission through multiple physical command posts. Every manual handoff introduced delays into the process, forcing capable and motivated paratroopers to spend precious time acting as data couriers and analysts.
Possible workarounds like quick-fire channels, introduced during our integration and testing efforts, shortened the kill chain by bypassing intermediate command posts to send missions directly to firing units. However, the underlying process remained unchanged as these nets still relied on voice communications, manual data transfers, and analog systems. Additionally, removing intermediate steps concentrated more traffic at the receiving end, increasing the burden on personnel processing fire missions and network congestion.
We found sensors, cloud services, targeting software, and fire direction systems were developed and fielded for different purposes, on different timelines, and with different technical interfaces. Connecting them required bespoke network configurations and data links, constant troubleshooting, and repeated testing before data could flow reliably and cleanly from one system to another. In 79 A.D., Gaius Plinius Secundus, known today as Pliny the Elder, was the supreme commander of the Roman imperial fleet, permanently stationed at Misenum near Naples. He died during the eruption of Vesuvius, after sailing across the bay on a valiant but unsuccessful rescue mission. Amid such heavy responsibilities, Pliny also wrote one of antiquity’s great encyclopedic works. He read and excerpted books of all kinds, and he knew something about Roman monuments. On the form and meaning of the triumphal arch, his explanation was characteristically blunt: “The point of columns with statues on top is to raise a man above other mortals. Monumental arches, a newer invention, mean the same thing.” (Columnarum ratio erat attolli super ceteros mortales, quod et arcus significant novicio invento.)
By Pliny’s day, Rome’s freestanding stone arches were already becoming associated with military victories and the emperors who won them. In the centuries that followed, that association grew stronger. The three best-known surviving arches in the city of Rome today are all within walking distance of one another. The Arch of Titus, erected in 81 A.D., commemorates Rome’s conquest of Jerusalem and destruction of its Jewish temple (the carved menorah is impossible to miss). The Arch of Septimius Severus, erected in 203 A.D., commemorates Severus’ victories over the Parthians from 194 to 195 and 197 to 199. And the Arch of Constantine, dedicated in 315 A.D., commemorates Constantine I’s victory over the rival emperor Maxentius in 312.
In the modern world, these famous examples have helped make the association between monumental arches, military victory, and imperial power especially strong, although — as we will see — the architectural form itself can carry other meanings.
This has always been true. Before Pliny’s time, back in the freer days of the Roman Republic, these monuments had a different name and somewhat wider associations. They were called fornices (vaults or arches), and some were simply magnificent exercises in massive self-advertisement. The historian Livy tells us of one general who returned victorious from Spain in 196 B.C. with an enormous quantity of booty. Without even bothering to seek a triumph, the formal military procession authorized by the Senate, the general simply used some of the spoils to erect three fornices at prominent locations around Rome and topped them with gilded statues.
Strictly speaking, then, his fornices weren’t triumphal arches. They do show, however, that even in republican Rome, a man on the make could use an arch for conspicuous self-advertisement.
The practice of building those fornices was perfectly respectable. The word’s later career was less so. Because prostitutes frequented the vaulted spaces of Roman cities, the word fornix, the singular of fornices, came to mean a brothel. From it developed the verb fornicari, “to visit a brothel,” and eventually fornicatio, and the meaning the word still carries in English today.
It is presumably for this reason that, under Rome’s first emperor Augustus (63 B.C. to 14 A.D.), the Republican fornix gave way to arcus in official usage. The new word meant both “arch” and “bow,” a resonance that scholars have connected with Apollo, whom Augustus presented as his patron deity. (Augustus, too, understood the value of a good brand.)
But Augustus did more than preside over a new name. He also built arches on an unprecedented scale and narrowed their focus. Six arches stood in Rome in 27 B.C., when he took power. By his death in 14 A.D., almost as many new monuments had been added, and Augustus was the patron or honoree of all of them.

Welcome to The Adversarial. Every other week, we’ll provide you with expert analysis on America’s greatest challengers: China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and jihadists. Read more below.***IranIn late September, U.S. and Iranian negotiators engaged in indirect talks for the first time since the memorandum of understanding they struck in June fell apart. On Oct. 8, U.S. President Donald Trump said “productive discussions” were underway. But it will take some doing to break the deadlock. Tehran’s offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week carries diminishing allure for Washington, as traffic through the chokepoint has trended upward. Also, Iran’s demand for upfront financial returns only underscores the growing economic strain the regime is facing under U.S. pressure, and Tehran continues to insist that any nonproliferation discussions should come after an initial stage provides access to financial assets and sanctions relief. Taken together, the Trump administration likely sees the proposition as far from satisfactory — requiring financial concessions that Washington is reluctant to concede and providing no guarantee of progress on resuming inspections or securing limits on Iran’s nuclear program. The heightened rate of attacks on vessels in recent days is likely Tehran’s way of signaling that it can still inject more volatility into the market, but that won’t be enough to force Washington into accepting Iranian terms. Furthermore, a window of opportunity for Iran will soon close, as the Trump administration is less likely to feel pressure to address high oil prices and an unpopular war after the midterm elections on Nov. 3.Aerial picture of Tehran, July 1, 2026. Image: Reza Ghanbarzadeh via Wikimedia CommonsChinaThe Sept. 23–25 Washington summit between Trump and Chinese General Secretary Xi Jinping featured pageantry and unusually high levels of diplomatic protocol but achieved little of clear substance. While the Chinese side had reason to celebrate

On Oct. 8, U.S. President Donald Trump said “productive discussions” were underway. But it will take some doing to break the deadlock. Tehran’s offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week carries diminishing allure for Washington, as traffic through the chokepoint has trended upward. Also, Iran’s demand for upfront financial returns only underscores the growing economic strain the regime is facing under U.S. pressure, and Tehran continues to insist that any nonproliferation discussions should come after an initial stage provides access to financial assets and sanctions relief. Taken together, the Trump administration likely sees the proposition as far from satisfactory — requiring financial concessions that Washington is reluctant to concede and providing no guarantee of progress on resuming inspections or securing limits on Iran’s nuclear program. The heightened rate of attacks on vessels in recent days is likely Tehran’s way of signaling that it can still inject more volatility into the market, but that won’t be enough to force Washington into accepting Iranian terms. deduped_items.title: A C-Section in Shackles: A Palestinian Woman’s Harrowing Birth in Israeli Detention
deduped_items.summary: Dana Joudeh was denied proper food and medical care throughout her pregnancy in an Israeli prison. She gave birth to a premature baby surrounded by armed guards. The post A C-Section in Shackles: A Palestinian Woman’s Harrowing Birth in Israeli Detention appeared first on The Intercept.
deduped_items.body_text:
Dana Joudeh was in shackles when she found out she was pregnant.
The 35-year-old from the West Bank city of Nablus was newly married and had just spent her first night in an Israeli prison. Israeli forces had arrested her without charges and put her under administrative detention, an arbitrary condition for holding Palestinians hostage. She lost consciousness in front of Israeli soldiers at Sharon Prison, a temporary detention facility in the city of Netanya, and they took her to a hospital blindfolded. There, with her hands and feet bound in chains, she was given a pregnancy test that came back positive.
Joudeh would never get to experience the joys and travails of pregnancy outside of prison. She was in Israeli custody from the moment she found out, until she gave birth.
Like Joudeh, pregnant Palestinian women arrested by Israeli security forces since October 7, 2023, are forced to endure a physically and medically complex process in conditions characterized by inadequate access to food, family visits, and medicine, as well as frequent reports of violence.
The total number of pregnancies in custody among the hundreds of women seized since October 7 is unknown, but Joudeh is only the second documented example of a woman who gave birth while under Israeli detention in nearly 17 years, according to Palestinian prisoners’ rights advocates. Many cases, advocates say, may have gone unreported.
The Intercept spoke to Joudeh through her sister, Maram, who sat with Joudeh by her side while sharing a detailed account of her sister’s six-month pregnancy, which ended in a premature cesarean section.
Corroborated by statements and reports published by the Palestinian Prisoners’ Society and the Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs, among others, Joudeh’s story offers a glimpse into what it’s like to go through pregnancy while locked in Israel’s prison system, where she struggled to obtain basic prenatal care and relied on other prisoners to share their already limited food.
“She went through every kind of suffering in there,” Maram said.
Israeli forces used sound grenades inside the prison, according to Joudeh’s family and her lawyer, Hassan Abbadi, who provides volunteer legal support for detained Palestinians. They said soldiers would force the women to lie face down on the floor.
“Female prisoners are subjected to all forms of violence and are deprived of the most basic rights,” said Abbadi, who regularly visits Palestinian women in Israeli prisons. He described shortages of underwear, attacks by police dogs, and strip searches, among other forms of mistreatment.
Joudeh’s pregnancy unfolded against a broader surge in Israeli arrests and violence across the occupied Palestinian territories. As of September, Israel was holding roughly 9,350 Palestinian prisoners and detainees, including 90 women and more than 350 children, according to Palestinian prisoners’ organizations. More than 3,100 of them are being held under administrative detention, without charge or trial.
For Joudeh, who was transferred to Damon Prison in Haifa soon after discovering she was pregnant, there was little effort to make accommodations for her pregnancy. According to Maram and Abbadi, the food was scarce and of poor quality, consisting usually of a slice of toast and lentils, chickpeas, or hummus. Sometimes, the prisoners received a few olives, and the other women incarcerated with Joudeh would offer a part of their own meager portions and give it to her.
In a small cell she shared with 13 other women, she discussed baby names with Manar Karaja, another detainee who was pregnant at the same time. According to Amany Sarahneh, the media director of the Palestinian Prisoners’ Society, Karaja was still pregnant and still in Israeli detention as of October 6.
As her pregnancy progressed, Joudeh grew increasingly worried about her baby. She repeatedly asked for medical tests to make sure that both she and the fetus were healthy, Maram said, but her requests

deduped_items.title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
deduped_items.summary: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in GazaThe Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”. Conti
deduped_items.body_text:
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.
“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.
“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.
Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.
“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.
“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.
“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.
The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.
“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”
Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.
The ICJ, a UN body, rules on disputes between states, while the international criminal court (ICC) investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of atrocities and other grave international crimes.
Hours after the announcement, the Trump administration unveiled broad new sanctions against the ICC, on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.
The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnece

deduped_items.title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
deduped_items.summary: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river floodingIsaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurri
deduped_items.body_text:
Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.
Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.
The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.
In Zimbabwe, a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure.
Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins.
The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health.
In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.

deduped_items.title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
deduped_items.summary: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in GazaThe Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”. deduped_items.body_text:
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.
“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.
“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.
Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.
“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.
“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.
“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.
The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.
“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”
Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.
The ICJ, a UN body, rules on disputes between states, while the international criminal court (ICC) investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of atrocities and other grave international crimes.
Hours after the announcement, the Trump administration unveiled broad new sanctions against the ICC, on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.

deduped_items.title: Moment sports broadcasters flee on live TV broadcast as 7.7-magnitude earthquake hits Panama
deduped_items.body_text:
Sports broadcasters were forced to drop their microphones and run for safety while live on TV, as a huge 7.7-magnitude earthquake struck Panama.
The powerful earthquake hit the region on Friday at around 1pm local time, sending tremors across the southern coast of the Central American nation and more than 80 aftershocks.
It struck the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in the central Herrera province and had a depth of 10km.
The US Tsunami warning system issued alerts for the eastern Pacific, including Mexico and Chile, but these have since been lifted.
There have been no reports of fatalities, but at least two people have been injured.
A video captured the moment sports broadcasters were forced to flee as the earthquake shook the entire building they were inside and eventually cut off the lights.
The five male presenters initially look at each other, confused as the walls and light fixtures behind them visibly start to shake.
But as the tremors continued and became more aggressive, some quickly put down their microphones, others simply taking the equipment with them, and jumped up to get out of the building to safety.
Five sports broadcasters were sat on stools live on TV when a 7.7-magnitude earthquake struck
They were seen looking puzzled and confused as the walls and light fittings began to shake and sway aggressively
Within minutes, they had fled with their microphones to safety
The US Geological Survey initially estimated it to be a magnitude-8.0 quake before revising it down to 7.7.
The powerful earthquake collapsed buildings and roads in the centre of the country yesterday, with the shallow tremor felt across the Central American nation of around 4.5million people, according to the National Civil Protection System.
The head of emergency operations Rene Garcia said that there had been no reports of fatalities so far.
In Panama City, about 200km from the epicentre, there were scenes of panic as people rushed to evacuate from the city's emblematic skyscrapers.
Salomon Andion, 46, had to evacuate his 15-storey building for the second time following aftershocks.
He said: 'I was scared because the shaking was very strong and prolonged.
'Heavy objects like dressers, the bed, and all the kitchen items were shaking.'
One video shared widely on social media showed water falling from the rooftop pool of a building more than 20 stories tall.
Cars were trapped underneath the rubble as the 7.7-magnitude earthquake struck the city of Penonome
St John the Baptist Cathedral in Penonome was severely damaged during the tremours
Another showed a bridge over the Panama Canal shaking violently, but remaining upright as vehicles travelled across it.
Panama's President Jose Raul Mulino said: 'We are facing a major disaster,' adding that some roads had 'completely collapsed.'
Juana Alveo, a 38-year-old cashier at a store in the city of Penonome in central Cocle province, said: 'It was horrible, like nothing we ever experienced. My daughter was trapped in school.'
The two injuries were reported by people trapped in different collapsed structures - one near a church in Veraguas, the other in a collapsed hotel in Cocle, authorities said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote on X on Friday that he was 'closely monitoring' the situation, with his office 'rapidly mobilizing resources and personnel to assist,' at the Panamanian government's request.
The Panama Canal Authority said shipping through the channel, which connects the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, was unaffected and operating 'as normal'.
Mulino travelled to Penonome to coordinate the disaster response.
Health Minister Fernando Boyd said that the most affected areas were the provinces of Herrera and Cocle, as well as Los Santos.
Rubble from the damaged buildings blocked roads in Panama after Friday's earthquake
One building entirely collapsed on one side, leaving cars buried beneath the debris

deduped_items.title: Kim Kardashian arrives in Singapore to cheer on boyfriend Lewis Hamilton - sparking Martin Brundle to make cheeky joke
deduped_items.body_text:
Kim Kardashian arrives in Singapore to cheer on boyfriend Lewis Hamilton - sparking Martin Brundle to make cheeky joke
Kim Kardashian arrived at the Singapore Grand Prix on Saturday to cheer on her F1 driver boyfriend Lewis Hamilton, prompting pundit Martin Brundle to make a joke about his last disastrous attempt to interview the influencer.
The businesswoman and reality star, 45, made sure to turn heads in the paddock with a £2,290 sheer pink maxi dress from French fashion house Alaia, which hugged her famous hourglass curves.
She accessorised perfectly with a matching Hermes Mini Kelly bag, adorned with silver charms, and chunky dark sunglasses.
The mother of four was flanked by two friends and a member of her security team while arriving at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.
Never one to blend into the background, Ms Kardashian attracted plenty of attention as fans unashamedly snapped pictures of her as she walked around.
Members of the media were quick to pick her out of the crowd and, when she appeared on screens, Sky Sport's Brundle joked: 'I did try once.'
He was referring to a previous attempt to speak to Ms Kardashian at the Monaco Grand Prix in June, when both she and her sister Khloe point-blank ignored him, prompting complaints from fans they had been 'rude'.
Kim Kardashian arrived in style at the Singapore Grand Prix to support her F1 driver boyfriend Lewis Hamilton
The businesswoman and influencer, 45, turned heads in a pastel pink figure-hugging dress from luxury brand Alaia, which she accessorised with black shades
Ms Kardashian was flanked by security guards and quickly attracted the attention of fans and photographers as she arrived
Hamilton and Ms Kardashian began dating in around February this year and have since gone Instagram-official.
The driver today competed in the Singapore Grand Prix's sprint race and was hoping to also qualify in the top few spots for Sunday's main event.
The course, which takes place through the city streets, brought a brand new concept to Formula 1 when it joined the calendar in 2008 due to it taking place at night.
Typically, a race weekend sees drivers undergo qualifying on Saturday before the main race takes place on Sunday.
But a recent addition to the sport's schedule now sees certain tracks hold sprints on Saturday too, which are around a third of the length of a full Grand Prix and see points handed out from eight to one for the top finishers.
Ahead of the planned sprint today, torrential rain forced it to be delayed as marshals were pictured frantically trying to sweep endless puddles of rain from the course.
The race eventually got underway at 10.30am, with Hamilton finishing second behind Red Bull's Max Verstappen.
She was accompanied by friends in the Ferrari garage, as she watched Hamilton in the sprint race where he finished second

deduped_items.title: Hot chocolate will be richer and creamier if you add 1 simple ingredient while making it
deduped_items.summary: Homemade chocolate can often turn out lumpy and bland, but there is a really easy way to make the best drink possible as you just need a common ingrifent you likely already have in your kitchen.
deduped_items.body_text:
Hot chocolate will be richer and creamier if you add 1 simple ingredient while making it
Homemade chocolate can often turn out lumpy and bland, but there is a really easy way to make the best drink possible as you just need a common ingrifent you likely already have in your kitchen.
Autumn is the cosiest time of year, when most of us simply want to snuggle up under a blanket with a indulgent hot chocolate to ward off the evening chill. And it's surprisingly straightforward to recreate that coffee shop quality at home — as long as you've got the right ingredients to hand.
Homemade hot chocolate can often turn out disappointingly flat, largely because most people simply stir the chocolate straight into the milk, which can make it cloyingly sweet and actually masks the rich chocolatey taste. If you want to nail the perfect cup every time, Ashley Manila, founder of Baker By Nature, has revealed that this much-loved warming drink benefits enormously from a simple addition — salt.
Ashley said: "A tiny pinch of salt wakes up the chocolate flavour and helps the drink from becoming too sweet. I like using Maldon sea salt, but any fine or flaky sea salt will work. If you're using flaky salt, simply crush it in your fingertips before adding."
Chocolate can be notoriously difficult to transform into a satisfying drink, as the sweetness often dominates, leaving you feeling overwhelmed after just a few sips.
Salt has a remarkable effect on your taste buds, amplifying certain flavours — which is precisely why it features so frequently in baked goods, where it draws out the depth and richness of chocolate, reports the Express.
It essentially allows the chocolate flavours to shine through rather than the sugar, resulting in a far creamier and more full-bodied drink. Adding a pinch of salt is a wonderfully cheap and straightforward way to take your hot chocolate to the next level, giving it that indulgent, coffee shop quality taste.
If you're using dark chocolate, salt works to dial down some of its natural bitterness while bringing out a deeper, richer flavour for a more intense chocolatey hit.
How to make the best hot chocolate
You will need:
- 600ml of whole milk
- 225ml of double cream
- Half a teaspoon of salt
- 227g of chocolate (chopped up)
- One tablespoon of icing sugar
- Two teaspoons of vanilla extract (optional)
- Pinch of cinnamon (optional)
Notes:
As a rule, it's best to opt for good-quality dark chocolate, as it lends a richer, more indulgent flavour to your drink.
Milk chocolate is perfectly fine if that's what you prefer, though it can occasionally make your hot chocolate overly sweet and can mask the other flavours. Ultimately, it comes down to personal taste — and if you can't make up your mind, simply go for half dark and half milk chocolate.
You can also finish off your hot chocolate with a dollop of whipped cream, chocolate shavings or a chocolate flake.
Method:
Start by placing a pan over a medium heat and adding the milk, cream, and salt. Heat the mixture until it begins to simmer, but take care not to let it come to a full boil.
Avoid cranking up the heat too high or allowing the mixture to bubble, as this will scorch the milk and leave your hot chocolate with an unpleasant grainy, lumpy texture.
Once the mixture is sufficiently warmed through, take it off the heat and stir in the chopped chocolate. Whisk thoroughly until it has melted completely into the liquid.
Return the pan to the heat and stir in the icing sugar, vanilla extract and cinnamon (if using). Keep whisking constantly for eight to 10 minutes until the mixture thickens nicely.
Once ready, simply pour into mugs and your gloriously rich, velvety hot chocolate is good to go. Finish with a generous dollop of whipped cream and a scattering of shaved chocolate to taste.

Autumn is the cosiest time of year, when most of us simply want to snuggle up under a blanket with a indulgent hot chocolate to ward off the evening chill. And it's surprisingly straightforward to recreate that coffee shop quality at home — as long as you've got the right ingredients to hand.
Homemade hot chocolate can often turn out disappointingly flat, largely because most people simply stir the chocolate straight into the milk, which can make it cloyingly sweet and actually masks the rich chocolatey taste. If you want to nail the perfect cup every time, Ashley Manila, founder of Baker By Nature, has revealed that this much-loved warming drink benefits enormously from a simple addition — salt.
Ashley said: "A tiny pinch of salt wakes up the chocolate flavour and helps the drink from becoming too sweet. I like using Maldon sea salt, but any fine or flaky sea salt will work. If you're using flaky salt, simply crush it in your fingertips before adding."
Chocolate can be notoriously difficult to transform into a satisfying drink, as the sweetness often dominates, leaving you feeling overwhelmed after just a few sips.
Salt has a remarkable effect on your taste buds, amplifying certain flavours — which is precisely why it features so frequently in baked goods, where it draws out the depth and richness of chocolate, reports the Express.
It essentially allows the chocolate flavours to shine through rather than the sugar, resulting in a far creamier and more full-bodied drink. Adding a pinch of salt is a wonderfully cheap and straightforward way to take your hot chocolate to the next level, giving it that indulgent, coffee shop quality taste.
If you're using dark chocolate, salt works to dial down some of its natural bitterness while bringing out a deeper, richer flavour for a more intense chocolatey hit.

- 600ml of whole milk
- 225ml of double cream
- Half a teaspoon of salt
- 227g of chocolate (chopped up)
- One tablespoon of icing sugar
- Two teaspoons of vanilla extract (optional)
- Pinch of cinnamon (optional)
Notes:

Milk chocolate is perfectly fine if that's what you prefer, though it can occasionally make your hot chocolate overly sweet and can mask the other flavours. Ultimately, it comes down to personal taste — and if you can't make up your mind, simply go for half dark and half milk chocolate.
You can also finish off your hot chocolate with a dollop of whipped cream, chocolate shavings or a chocolate flake.
Method:
Start by placing a pan over a medium heat and adding the milk, cream, and salt. Heat the mixture until it begins to simmer, but take care not to let it come to a full boil.
Avoid cranking up the heat too high or allowing the mixture to bubble, as this will scorch the milk and leave your hot chocolate with an unpleasant grainy, lumpy texture.
Once the mixture is sufficiently warmed through, take it off the heat and stir in the chopped chocolate. Whisk thoroughly until it has melted completely into the liquid.
Return the pan to the heat and stir in the icing sugar, vanilla extract and cinnamon (if using). Keep whisking constantly for eight to 10 minutes until the mixture thickens nicely.
Once ready, simply pour into mugs and your gloriously rich, velvety hot chocolate is good to go. Finish with a generous dollop of whipped cream and a scattering of shaved chocolate to taste.

deduped_items.title: “Cult of Death”? Check your calling card, Mr. Rubio
deduped_items.summary: TEHRAN — US Secretary of State Marco Rubio addressed Iran in parts of his Wednesday evening speech at the Acropolis in Athens. Taken as a whole, his speech was a selective reading of history; a flimsy version of Samuel Huntington's "Clash of Civilizations." When the argument is flimsy, a theatrical stage must inevitably be built out of historical symbols. The audience is meant to be impressed by the backdrop, not by the force of the reasoning.

deduped_items.title: Iran turns to Turkey, Turkmenistan for power as war strains industry
deduped_items.summary: Iran is seeking more electricity from Turkey and Turkmenistan as war damage and other outages leave thousands of megawatts of industrial and petrochemical power capacity offline, even as Washington presses neighboring countries to help restrict Tehran’s remaining economic routes.
deduped_items.body_text:
Trump said on Truth Social that Washington was having “productive discussions” with Iran and would not attack the country before the November 3 elections. He said, however, that the US blockade of Iranian ports would remain in place.
Trump had made similar remarks ahead of previous military action against Iran. In June 2025, he said he would decide within two weeks whether the United States would join Israel’s war against Iran, citing a “substantial chance” of negotiations. US forces struck Iranian nuclear sites days later. 
Also days before the 2026 war, Trump said he preferred a diplomatic solution with Iran while also laying out the case for possible military action.
The remarks offered the clearest timeline yet for a pause in renewed US strikes, while leaving open the possibility of military action after the elections.
On the Iranian side, President Masoud Pezeshkian said during a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin that Tehran had not left the negotiating table and was working on its response to the latest US proposal.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi provided further detail Thursday, saying Iran had received Washington’s response to Tehran’s “seven-day plan” and was reviewing it.
Araghchi said Tehran would deliver its response within the next few days and that messages continued to pass between Iran and the United States through mediators.
Reports of US military preparations
The talks are continuing as Washington prepares for the possibility of renewed military action.
Senior US officials told Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir earlier this week that the White House and Pentagon had instructed US forces to prepare for a possible large-scale attack on Iran within the next three weeks, Israel’s Channel 12 reported Thursday.
The network cited a senior US official and another source briefed on the conversation. Zamir warned that an attack within that timeframe could lead to the postponement of Israel’s October 27 election, based on an assessment that Iran would respond with heavy missile fire against Israel.
Trump’s pledge not to strike Iran before the US midterms appears to rule out that timeline, but does not remove the prospect of renewed military action after the November 3 vote.
No boots on the ground
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Thursday Washington was not seeking to “nation build” in Iran or deploy large numbers of ground troops to control territory, framing the US objective as preventing Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
Hegseth said Iran could achieve that outcome “the easy way or the hard way,” but that Trump would ultimately decide how to proceed. If military action became necessary, he said, it would be “swift and decisive.”
Mediators are also seeking more room for diplomacy. They have asked Trump to give them additional time for negotiations before any potential attack on Iran, Al Hadath reported Thursday, citing a US source.
In his meeting with Putin, Iran’s Pezeshkian said there was no end to the war in sight as long as the United States continued what he described as unilateralism.
Iranian Defense Ministry spokesperson Reza Talaei-Nik also told the state TV that the country’s arms-production capacity was sufficient to sustain a prolonged war.
“We currently have the production capacity needed for a sustained and prolonged war within our production system,” Talaei-Nik added. 
He said Defense Ministry personnel were working alongside missile launch crews, drone units and Revolutionary Guards and army naval and air forces to use battlefield experience to upgrade weapons and equipment based on emerging threats.
Hormuz remains a flashpoint
Iran’s warnings also focused on the Strait of Hormuz, a key issue in negotiations with Washington.
Revolutionary Guards commander-in-chief Ahmad Vahidi said Thursday that the United States and other “extra-regional” powers had no right to interfere in the strait or the Persian Gulf, warning that threats or unauthorized naval movements would face a forceful re

Also days before the 2026 war, Trump said he preferred a diplomatic solution with Iran while also laying out the case for possible military action.
The remarks offered the clearest timeline yet for a pause in renewed US strikes, while leaving open the possibility of military action after the elections.
On the Iranian side, President Masoud Pezeshkian said during a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin that Tehran had not left the negotiating table and was working on its response to the latest US proposal.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi provided further detail Thursday, saying Iran had received Washington’s response to Tehran’s “seven-day plan” and was reviewing it.

The network cited a senior US official and another source briefed on the conversation. Zamir warned that an attack within that timeframe could lead to the postponement of Israel’s October 27 election, based on an assessment that Iran would respond with heavy missile fire against Israel.

خرجت في بلجيكا مظاهرة نظمتها النقابات العمالية، تطالب الحكومة بوقف خطتها القائمة على الحد من القدرة الشرائية للمواطنين، مقدمة بديلا يوفر للحكومة 21 مليار يورو (نحو 22.7 مليار دولار) لموازنة العام المقبل.

deduped_items.title: US FCC plan to bar Chinese testing labs could disrupt global electronics supply chains, raise industry costs: analysts
deduped_items.body_text:
US FCC plan to bar Chinese testing labs could disrupt global electronics supply chains, raise industry costs: analysts
The seal of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) prior to an open commission meeting at the agency's headquarters in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, Feb. 18, 2026. Photo: VCG
A US plan to bar Chinese laboratories from testing electronic devices for the American market could disrupt a key link in the global electronics supply chain, potentially forcing manufacturers to move testing operations overseas and raising costs for an industry heavily reliant on China's manufacturing and testing capabilities, Chinese analysts said on Thursday.
The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that it will vote on October 29 on a proposal to bar laboratories and certification bodies in countries including China that do not offer reciprocal treatment to US-based labs from conducting FCC-required testing, Reuters reported.
The proposed restrictions, covering devices such as smartphones, computers and cameras destined for the US market, are scheduled to take effect in December 2028 if approved.
The proposal would widen restrictions introduced in 2025, when the FCC barred laboratories owned or controlled by the Chinese government from testing electronics for the US market, affecting several dozen facilities. The agency said this year, however, that a substantial majority of China-based labs continued to conduct such testing, according to Reuters.
He Weiwen, a senior fellow at the Center for China and Globalization, told the Global Times on Thursday that the proposed ban marks a further expansion of the FCC's technology restrictions on China, extending beyond telecom operators and equipment to testing and certification services.
"The move reflects an attempt to suppress China's role in the telecommunications sector, driven by concerns over the competitive disadvantage of the US relative to China in these areas," the expert said, describing the measure as a non-market, protectionist approach to technological competition.
According to the Reuters report, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said that 82 percent of electronic devices covered by the agency's testing figures were tested in China in 2025, while fewer than 4 percent were tested in US-based laboratories.
Under the proposal, manufacturers relying on China-based labs for FCC testing would need to shift to facilities in the US or other eligible economies. In a proposed rule published in the US Federal Register in May, the FCC sought public comment on ways to mitigate transition costs, as well as possible additional fees and oversight requirements.
The concentration of testing in China reflects the close integration of electronics manufacturing and compliance testing, an arrangement that global manufacturers have benefited from for years, with nearby laboratories helping reduce logistics costs and shorten development cycles, according to international testing firm Element.
Element also warned that shifting testing to other approved laboratories could lead to longer lead times and higher costs as demand puts pressure on available capacity. Manufacturers could also face greater scheduling difficulties and reduced access to specialized testing expertise, particularly for less common types of testing.
He Weiwen cautioned that placing national security considerations above objective technological principles could hinder technological progress and harm economic efficiency.
The proposal is the latest in a series of FCC restrictions affecting Chinese technology. The agency blocked approval of new models of Chinese-made drones in December 2025 and foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026. It also expanded equipment restrictions involving Huawei and ZTE in June and moved in July to bar devices containing key components from Chinese firms under the pretext of so-called national security risks.

deduped_items.title: South Africa freedom day memorial gathering reveals its pursuit of dignity and inclusive governance in post apartheid era
deduped_items.body_text:
IN-DEPTH / IN-DEPTH
South Africa freedom day memorial gathering reveals its pursuit of dignity and inclusive governance in post apartheid era
Politics finds its rhythm
 Editor's Note: 
In an era of profound global shifts and increasingly complex regional dynamics, a proper understanding of the world must be rooted in "grounded experience" and localized insights. Global Times English edition, in collaboration with the Academy of International and Regional Communication Studies, Communication University of China, is proud to launch "Local Insights," an English-language column dedicated to original, field-based observations.
We invite Chinese scholars and professionals who are studying, conducting exchanges, or working outside China, as well as international students and friends living and studying in China who are familiar with the social contexts of their home countries or third countries, to begin from first-hand field experience and engage with social, cultural, and contemporary issues beyond China. In the fifth article of this column, drawing on her onâtheâground experience as a Chinese exchange scholar, the author observes a South Africa Freedom Day memorial gathering, revealing how local politics unfolds through collective singing, dancing, and grassroots participation, while also reflecting on the gap between political liberation and economic justice.
As a PhD student, I am currently on an exchange program at Nelson Mandela University in South Africa, with support from the China Scholarship Council. Since arriving here, I have developed a habit of stepping beyond campus whenever possible. Community meetings, municipal events and public gatherings have become a vital way for me to engage with local life. This time, a local friend recommended that I attend a memorial event in Kariega, organized by the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU) in honor of its former president, Phumzile John Gomomo. Beyond that, I had little sense of what kind of gathering I was about to enter.
It was on the way that I noticed the streets were unusually vibrant. Groups of people were dressed in colorful attire, with bright Xhosa headscarves and garments bearing political symbols. My friend then reminded me that it was April 27, which is Freedom Day in South Africa. On this day in 1994, South Africa held its first non-racial election, formally ending apartheid and inaugurating democratic rule. Over the past three decades, Freedom Day commemorates political liberation, while also inviting recurring reflection on whether the promise of freedom has been fully realized. In that sense, Freedom Day marks an important moment for observing contemporary South African politics and social sentiment.
The aerial view of Johannesburg, South Africa Photo: VCG
From street to hall: Entering Freedom Day
The event was scheduled to begin at 10 am, and we arrived shortly before the hour. Yet there were not many people present. Banners of COSATU, the South African Communist Party (SACP), and the African National Congress (ANC) had already been displayed inside the hall, quietly framing the political context of the gathering. Although my understanding was still limited, I could already sense that their presence mattered. COSATU, SACP and ANC represent key forces in South Africa's political landscape, historically linked through the "Tripartite Alliance" formed during the anti-apartheid struggle and sustained in various forms since 1994. I could see that this was not simply a local gathering, but one embedded within a much longer political tradition.
What struck me first was how different the atmosphere was from what I had expected of a political gathering. There was no sense of urgency or visible tension. My friend introduced me around, and we greeted each other through handshakes, embraces and brief conversations, with a familiarity that suggested long-standing connections. deduped_items.title: China to introduce new train timetable from July 1, including high-speed train service between Beijing and Urumqi
deduped_items.body_text:
China to introduce new train timetable from July 1, including high-speed train service between Beijing and Urumqi
Passengers are pictured at the Beijing Tongzhou Railway Station in the Beijing Municipal Administrative Center in Beijing, capital of China, May 29, 2026. From 2016 to 2026, the Beijing Municipal Administrative Center marks a decade of planning and development. Over the past ten years, it has undergone a remarkable transformation into a vibrant modern area. Photo: Xinhua
China's national railway network will implement a new train-running timetable starting July 1, which will strengthen connectivity between the country's northwestern provinces and the central, southern, and southwestern regions, while also introducing high-speed train service for the first time between Urumqi, Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, and Beijing, the China State Railway Group announced on Wednesday.
Tickets under the new timetable went on sale on Wednesday.
The upgraded network is expected to further enhance railway transportation capacity and operational efficiency. Under the new timetable, China's national railways will operate 12,174 scheduled passenger trains, marking an increase of 106 trains compared with the current schedule.
For example, the railway authorities have arranged 58 high-speed trains from Xi'an in Northwest China's Shaanxi to destinations including Nanyang of Central China's Henan Province, Hankou of Central China's Hubei Province and Chongqing city in Southwest China.
Wan Yaqiong, director of the ticket sales workshop at Xi'an Station under China Railway Xi'an Group, said that the new timetable will introduce direct services from Xi'an to Hankou, with the fastest round-trip travel time controlled within seven hours, according to a report by the China Central Television (CCTV) News on Wednesday.
Additionally, high-speed trains will operate from Yan'an city in Shaanxi to Shaoshan city in Central China's Hunan, establishing a direct high-speed rail link between the two major "red tourism" destinations - historical sites with a modern revolutionary legacy, the CCTV News report noted.
After the timetable adjustment, high-speed trains will run for the first time between Urumqi station and Beijing West station. At the same time, the T-series trains operating between Urumqi and Chongqing West will be upgraded to Z-series direct express trains, shortening the travel time between the two places by more than two hours.
The railway authorities will increase the number of high-speed services during morning and evening rush hours on certain high-speed rail lines in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, the Yangtze River Delta, and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, providing greater convenience for commuters.

deduped_items.summary: 新华社合肥6月5日电 中共中央政治局委员、国务院副总理刘国中3日至5日到安徽调研“三夏”农业生产工作。他强调，要深入学习贯彻习近平总书记关于国家粮食安全的重要论述，按照党中央、国务院部署，扛稳政治责任，毫不放松抓好夏收夏种夏管，全力以赴夺取夏粮丰收，全面打牢秋粮生产基础，确保完成全年粮食生产目标任务。 刘国中先后来到宿州市、淮南市、六安市，深入小麦机收和夏播现场、农机跨区作业服务点、农事服务中心、粮食仓储中心、地方农科院等，实地察看夏收夏种、农机作业服务保障、粮食烘干收储等工作，详细了解农作物新品种选育、大面积单产提升、农资保供稳价、高标准农田建设等情况。 刘国中强调，“三夏”工作抓得好不好，事关全年粮食生产目标任务能否顺利实现。当前正值“三夏”农业生产关键时期，要抓住有利天气抢晴收获，组织好农机跨区作业，强化服务保障和安全管理，确保夏收高效进行。要抓实抓牢机收减损、烘干晾晒等各项措施，最大程度减少粮食损失。要精心做好夏粮收购工作，引导各类企业积极入市，保障粮食市场平稳运行。要压茬推进夏播，加强农资供应和农事服务，强化技术集成及推广应用，落实落细合理密植、精量播种等大面积单产提升措施，

deduped_items.summary: 大美中国，江山如画。 党的十八大以来，习近平总书记的考察足迹遍及神州大地。祁连山麓、坝上林海，秦岭深处、黄河之滨，总书记在大江奔涌处谋划千秋大计，在山川锦绣间擘画生态蓝图。一系列重要论述，为新时代生态文明建设提供了根本遵循和行动指南。 世界环境日到来之际，我们跟随习近平总书记的脚步，一起呵护山水、寄情山水，领悟守护绿水青山、建设生态文明之道。 江河为脉 心系长江之变，习近平总书记前往沿江重镇，考察长江经济带发展。从三峡库区到洞庭湖畔，从港口码头到企业车间，总书记深入调研，作出一系列重要指示，为新时代江河保护治理提供了重要遵循。 2018年4月，习近平总书记来到湖南岳阳城陵矶水文站考察。在狭窄的站房外长廊上，习近平总书记举目远眺。“共抓大保护，不搞大开发”的战略定力，在这里化作守护一江碧水的坚定行动。 2023年10月10日下午，习近平总书记在江西九江市考察，冒雨在江边察看，了解当地长江国家文化公园建设、长江岸线生态修复等情况。10月12日，总书记在进一步推动长江经济带高质量发展座谈会上回顾长江经济带发展历程，感慨：“做就要做好，坚定做下去。笃行不怠，一以贯之，久久为功。” 黄河安澜是中

deduped_items.title: 国务院印发《关于开展第四次全国农业普查的通知》
deduped_items.summary: 新华社北京6月5日电 国务院日前印发《关于开展第四次全国农业普查的通知》（以下简称《通知》）。根据《中华人民共和国统计法》和《全国农业普查条例》规定，国务院决定于2026年开展第四次全国农业普查。 《通知》强调，第四次全国农业普查是在以中国式现代化全面推进中华民族伟大复兴的新征程上开展的一项重大国情国力调查，要以习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想为指导，深入贯彻党的二十大和二十届二中、三中全会精神，认真落实党中央、国务院决策部署，坚持依法普查、科学普查、为民普查，坚持实事求是、守正创新，全面摸清新时代我国“三农”家底，客观反映农业发展新情况、乡村建设新面貌、农民生活新变化、农村改革新成效。 《通知》指出，第四次全国农业普查的对象是在中华人民共和国境内的农村住户，包括农村农业生产经营户和其他住户；城镇农业生产经营户；农业生产经营单位；村民委员会；乡镇人民政府。普查的主要内容包括农业生产条件、粮食和大食物生产情况、农业新质生产力情况、乡村发展基本情况、农村居民生活情况等。普查的标准时点为2026年12月31日24时，时期资料为2026年年度资料。 《通知》要求，各地区、各部门要按照全国统一领

deduped_items.summary: 新华社北京6月5日电 近日，中共中央办公厅印发《党组讨论和决定党员处分事项工作程序规定》，并发出通知，要求各地区各部门认真遵照执行。 《党组讨论和决定党员处分事项工作程序规定》全文如下。 党组讨论和决定党员处分事项工作程序规定 （2018年11月29日中共中央批准 2018年11月29日中共中央办公厅发布 2025年5月26日中共中央修订 2025年5月26日中共中央办公厅发布） 第一条 为了规范党组讨论和决定党员处分事项，根据《中国共产党党组工作条例》、《中国共产党处分违纪党员批准权限和程序规定》，制定本规定。 第二条 坚持用改革精神和严的标准管党治党，落实党组（含党组性质党委，下同）全面从严治党主体责任，强化纪检监察机关派驻机构（以下简称派驻机构）监督职责，始终以严的基调、严的措施、严的氛围纵深推进正风肃纪反腐。 第三条 对党组管理的人员中的党员实施党纪处分，党组、纪委监委派出的纪检监察工委（以下简称派出机构）、派驻机构等应当按照规定权限和程序履行职责，加强协调沟通，有序顺畅衔接，形成工作合力，实现政治效果、纪法效果和社会效果有机统一。 第四条 党组讨论和决定本单位党员党纪处分事项

deduped_items.summary: 大美中国，江山如画。 党的十八大以来，习近平总书记的考察足迹遍及神州大地。祁连山麓、坝上林海，秦岭深处、黄河之滨，总书记在大江奔涌处谋划千秋大计，在山川锦绣间擘画生态蓝图。一系列重要论述，为新时代生态文明建设提供了根本遵循和行动指南。 世界环境日到来之际，我们跟随习近平总书记的脚步，一起呵护山水、寄情山水，领悟守护绿水青山、建设生态文明之道。 江河为脉 心系长江之变，习近平总书记前往沿江重镇，考察长江经济带发展。从三峡库区到洞庭湖畔，从港口码头到企业车间，总书记深入调研，作出一系列重要指示，为新时代江河保护治理提供了重要遵循。 2018年4月，习近平总书记来到湖南岳阳城陵矶水文站考察。在狭窄的站房外长廊上，习近平总书记举目远眺。“共抓大保护，不搞大开发”的战略定力，在这里化作守护一江碧水的坚定行动。 2023年10月10日下午，习近平总书记在江西九江市考察，冒雨在江边察看，了解当地长江国家文化公园建设、长江岸线生态修复等情况。10月12日，总书记在进一步推动长江经济带高质量发展座谈会上回顾长江经济带发展历程，感慨：“做就要做好，坚定做下去。笃行不怠，一以贯之，久久为功。” 黄河安澜是中

deduped_items.title: 多地升级信用修复服务 助力经营主体重塑良好信用
deduped_items.summary: 健全信用修复制度是经营主体信用体系建设的重要内容，是当事人申请解除惩戒措施、重塑信用的制度保障。今年以来，多地深入贯彻党中央、国务院关于全面深化改革、优化营商环境的决策部署，推动企业数据填报“高效办成一件事”和市场监管领域统一信用修复落地见效。 多地完善相关政策 2021年8月，市场监管总局公布《市场监督管理信用修复管理办法》，推动解决信息公示期限较长、信用修复机制不健全等问题。今年以来，在全面深化改革、优化营商环境的大背景下，信用修复再次成为高频词。 在北京，为进一步优化营商环境，北京市市场监管局自2025年起全面升级信用修复服务，通过机制创新、流程优化、精准帮扶等创新举措，今年第一季度已助力6万户企业通过信用修复重塑良好信用。北京市市场监管局信用处副处长丁学雷介绍，为帮助经营主体纾困解难，激发市场活力，北京市市场监管局建立健全常态化信用修复机制，依法依规实现“能修必修、应修尽修”，助力经营主体重塑良好信用。 在江西，各级市场监管部门积极宣传推广市场监管信用修复全国统一平台，引导经营主体通过该平台申请信用修复，并探索推行容缺受理、并联修复等模式，利用各渠道精准推送修复提醒，切实为经营

deduped_items.title: 河南卢氏：“小议事”撬动“大治理”
deduped_items.summary: 在树下院落、乡间凉亭，一场场热气腾腾的“凉亭夜话”，正悄然改变着河南省三门峡市卢氏县基层治理的面貌。从群众自发到如今党委引领下的制度化实践，“凉亭夜话”不仅成为群众表达心声的平台，也构建起基层治理的创新模式，让“小议事”撬动“大治理”。 “凉亭夜话”源于卢氏县木桐乡群众的自发行动。农闲时，村民围坐凉亭、树下，或为化解纠纷说和相劝，或为某一项目献计献策。卢氏县党委因势利导，对此进行规范化、制度化，并在全县推广。 “凉亭夜话”以开放空间为议事场景，每月至少组织一次群众议事会，激发群众参与热情。同时，明确“五议三不议”原则，划定议事边界。通过建立民情收集机制，形成“民情清单”“议事清单”，配套“四公”议事制度和闭环工作机制，加强督促督办。 2024年，“凉亭夜话”决议落实率高达92%，持续激发干部群众谋发展、干事业、促振兴的内生动力。木桐乡年投资59亿元的钼矿项目落地，创办了创业技能培训中心，打造了“灵神粉条”网红品牌，办起了位于豫陕交界地带的烤鱼店，各项产业红红火火，名列全县“十快乡镇”。全县农村党支部领办专业合作社170余家，涌现出一批集体经济收入超百万元的村。（记者 崔志坚 通讯员 刘

deduped_items.title: 聚力为民解难题办实事
deduped_items.summary: 【锲而不舍落实中央八项规定精神】 “现在回家再也不用为停车发愁了！收费实惠、管理规范，连周边环境都焕然一新。”近日，湖南省长沙市长沙县泉塘街道楠竹园社区的居民刘琴欣喜地发现，枫树路已实现华丽蝶变：往日拥堵的路面变得井然有序，志愿者在引导有序停车，崭新的人行护栏让居民出行更安全。 这条日均车流量超5000辆次的社区主动脉——枫树路，曾长期陷入停车困局：机动车“叠罗汉”式违停，电动车“见缝插针”占道，行人被迫与车争道，严重影响了社区形象和交通安全环境，基层治理面临严峻考验。 群众所急就是党员干部的行动号角。楠竹园社区经过集中走访了解到枫树路与盼盼路交会处有一处2500平方米的闲置地，果断制定解决方案：对这一地块进行整治，同时规范为停车场，进行收费管理，并在推进过程中打出治理“组合拳”：街道（社区）、交警、市政、物业公司、居民代表“1+5+N”协同机制，组建“节节高”党群先锋队，召开5场“竹邻”议事会，绘制出停车治理“作战图”。 短短一周时间，这片杂乱的闲置地已改造成便民停车场，场内增设智能道闸系统，增加停车位300余个，收费标准低于市场价20%，切实缓解了片区“车多位少”的停车困境。 深入
