deduped_items.title: Abbas postpones Palestinian elections, sets presidential poll for September 2027
deduped_items.summary: RAMALLAH, Oct 10 - Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday cancelled legislative elections scheduled for November due to worsening conditions within the Palestinian territories and set a date of September 11, 2027 for both presidential and legislative elections, the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.
deduped_items.body_text:
Abbas postpones Palestinian elections, sets presidential poll for September 2027
RAMALLAH, Oct 10 - Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday cancelled legislative elections scheduled for November due to worsening conditions within the Palestinian territories and set a date of September 11, 2027 for both presidential and legislative elections, the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.
Abbas' decree cited "obstacles posed by Israeli measures" to holding elections in November and the need to establish suitable political, security and on-the-ground conditions for "free, fair and inclusive elections". It called on Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza to participate in the polls.
There had been serious doubts that the Palestinian Authority vote would go ahead in late November. The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-06, after which Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas' rival, the Islamist group Hamas, seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists.
The decree said Israeli military attacks, settlement expansion, settler violence and movement restrictions in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, along with Israel's continued withholding of Palestinian tax revenues, created challenges to preparing for and holding elections on the previous date.
In Gaza, the decree pointed to "exceptional security and humanitarian conditions", the incomplete withdrawal of Israeli forces, the lack of progress in reconstruction and the failure to implement arrangements for deploying international stabilisation forces and police.
Israeli restrictions on access for election commission staff and international observers to Gaza and East Jerusalem also complicated preparations, the decree said.
The decision to postpone followed a resolution by the Palestine Liberation Organisation's executive committee and consultations with Palestinian factions and political forces. It also aimed to allow time for a comprehensive Palestinian national dialogue to strengthen unity and address challenges facing the electoral process. REUTERS

deduped_items.title: Strait war risk exaggerated: US official
deduped_items.body_text:
- Strait war risk exaggerated: US official A SHARED GOAL: The US and China do not want conflict, US diplomat Michael DeSombre said, adding that Xi was a ‘rational actor’ who calculates strategic risks
  - Staff writer, with CNA
Global investors are overestimating the likelihood of a conflict across the Taiwan Strait by next year, a senior US diplomat told CNBC on Thursday, adding that robust cross-strait deterrence and the prospect of severe repercussions would prevent Beijing from acting. Markets have exaggerated reports that Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) has instructed the Chinese People’s Liberation Army to be prepared for an invasion of Taiwan by next year, US Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific Affairs Michael DeSombre said. “I actually think the most mispricing is with regard to Taiwan, where actually I think people are overpricing the risk of something happening across the Taiwan Strait,” DeSombre said, expressing confidence that diplomatic and military deterrence would hold. US Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific Affairs Michael DeSombre speaks during a ceremony in Washington on July 27. Photo: EPA / Yonhap “Both China and the US don’t want conflict, and we’re able to deter conflict,” he said, adding that market anxieties are “priced at too high a level.” Xi is a “rational actor” who calculates strategic risks, he said. “To the extent that he realizes that it can’t be done, or it can’t be done without substantial consequences, it won’t happen,” he added. Separately, the US Department of State on Thursday described China’s activities in the east of Taiwan as deeply destabilizing and urged Beijing to stop pressuring Taipei, following a report of a Chinese maritime militia boat in the area in August. “[The US] remains concerned by China’s activity east of Taiwan,” a department spokesperson said. “China’s actions are deeply destabilizing. By asserting authorities around maritime areas that Taiwan has peacefully administered for over 70 years, China only exacerbates tensions and undermines the peaceful resolution of issues that it claims to seek.” They also urged Beijing to engage in meaningful dialogue with Taipei’s democratically elected authorities. The statement followed a Reuters report on Thursday that a Chinese maritime militia boat, the Minfudingyu 07902 (閩福鼎漁07902), had been spotted by Apex Aviation more than 30 nautical miles (55.6km) off Hualien County in mid-August. The Minfudingyu, which Apex identified as a fishing vessel that doubles as a Chinese maritime militia vessel, was accompanied by a China Coast Guard cutter and a research vessel at the time, Reuters said. The Ministry of National Defense said China was using law enforcement and scientific research as pretexts to expand its activities without triggering a conflict, create the impression that it had jurisdiction over the waters and challenge Taiwan’s maritime law enforcement authority. The Coast Guard Administration said all the Chinese vessels in question were operating outside Taiwan’s restricted waters and that it had monitored their movements throughout and responded appropriately.

deduped_items.title: King Mswati III pledges deeper Taiwan-Eswatini ties
deduped_items.body_text:
- King Mswati III pledges deeper Taiwan-Eswatini ties
  - Staff writer, with Reuters and CNA
Eswatini’s king yesterday pledged to deepen his country’s “enduring friendship” with Taiwan during a return visit to Taipei after President William Lai’s (賴清德) trip to the southern African nation in May that China tried to block. King Mswati III arrived early yesterday for a state visit until Saturday next week. He is to attend today’s Double Ten National Day celebrations in Taipei. The trip is his 20th visit to Taiwan and comes as the two countries celebrate 58 years of diplomatic ties. President William Lai, front left, welcomes King Mswati III of Eswatini, front right, with full military honors at Liberty Square in Taipei yesterday. Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times Eswatini would continue to advocate for Taiwan’s meaningful participation in the UN, the monarch said. “We deeply value the enduring friendship and cooperation between our two countries, and we look forward to strengthening these bonds for the benefit of our peoples,” the king told a welcoming ceremony on Liberty Square. Lai said the two sides had always collaborated from a position of trust and were partners who “support each other and grow together.” Cooperation with Eswatini has expanded under Taiwan’s diplomatic initiative to promote shared prosperity with its allies, with increasingly close exchanges between the two countries’ peoples, Lai said. In separate remarks, Lai thanked the king for supporting the establishment of a Taiwan Industrial Innovation Park in Eswatini and expressed hope that more Taiwanese companies would invest there, making the country a gateway to African markets. The two leaders also witnessed the signing of an agreement on mutual legal assistance in criminal matters, which Lai described as a milestone in law enforcement cooperation. Mswati emphasized turning existing bilateral agreements into practical cooperation and encouraging partnerships between businesses. “We need to put them into action,” he said, calling for officials to study how the agreements could be implemented effectively. Mswati’s itinerary includes observing a joint ground-air military exercise alongside Lai, a visit to an agricultural research center and an investment dinner hosted by Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍), the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said. Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Mao Ning (毛寧) said the king was interfering in China’s internal affairs and “ignoring the long-term interests of his people.” The former Swaziland is one of just 12 small states, mostly in Latin America, the Caribbean and the Pacific, that have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan. In April, Taiwan accused China of pressuring three other African countries to block overflight permission for Lai’s aircraft, causing him to postpone a plan to join celebrations of the 40th anniversary of the king’s accession. That was the first time a Taiwanese president had canceled an entire foreign trip due to denial of airspace access, an apparent new Chinese strategy to curb the nation’s international ties. Lai made a surprise trip in May, using an “arrive, then announce” approach.

deduped_items.title: Taiwan offers much more than tech, Tsai Ing-wen says
deduped_items.body_text:
- Taiwan offers much more than tech, Tsai Ing-wen says THREATS: Democracies face domestic divisions, outside authoritarian influence and technology that make it easy to spread disinformation across borders, the ex-president said
  - Staff writer, with CNA, SAN FRANCISCO
Taiwan offers the global democratic community much more than just semiconductors, former president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) told an audience at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution in San Francisco on Thursday, while defending her “boring” leadership style as a necessary asset to find common ground. Tsai spoke about how Taiwan has managed differences, responded to crises and built societal resilience. Discussions about Taiwan often focus on semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI), cross-strait relations, the risk of conflict and occasionally touch on its popular food and drinks, she said. Former president Tsai Ing-wen points to a drawing of herself at the Startup Island Taiwan Silicon Valley Hub in Palo Alto, California, on Thursday. Photo: CNA However, those topics are only part of the story, Tsai said, pointing to the nation’s 23 million people and their experience of building a democracy under challenging circumstances. “That experience has shaped who we are and continues to shape how we approach the future,” she said. Democracies face growing challenges from outside and within, as increasingly sophisticated authoritarian influence campaigns coincide with domestic populism and political polarization, she said. The domestic divisions make it harder to reach a consensus on how to respond to outside threats, she added. Tsai also warned that advances in AI have lowered language barriers, making it easier to spread disinformation across borders. “Ill-intentioned actors, especially from outside, use social media platforms to spread false and misleading information to drive a wedge between fellow citizens, between societies and their governments, and even between countries,” she said. However, decades of external pressure and intense domestic political competition have taught Taiwan how to safeguard democracy while keeping its institutions open and its society resilient, Tsai said. Taiwan has moved from authoritarian rule to its first direct presidential election in 1996 to become the vibrant democracy it is today, she said. “That transition taught us how to confront deep political differences without allowing those differences to make democratic progress impossible,” she said. Managing relations with China has required preparedness and restraint, Tsai said, adding that decades of pressure from Beijing have made Taiwan more resilient and pragmatic. Although Taiwanese hold differing views on what form relations with China should take, there is a consensus on maintaining the cross-strait “status quo,” avoiding unnecessary provocation, and protecting Taiwan’s democracy and security, she said. “Democracy, resilience and partnership are the foundation of our collective future,” Tsai said, adding that no amount of threats or coercion would shake Taiwan’s determination to engage with and contribute to the world. While some people described her as “boring” during her time as president, Tsai said that “being boring can be useful” in an era of increasing political polarization in which provocation attracts more attention than restraint. This is especially true when needing to ensure Taiwan’s security while finding enough common ground to keep democracy moving forward, she added. Tsai arrived in the US on Monday and is scheduled to return to Taiwan tomorrow. Additional reporting by Su Yung-yao

Hong Kong police have arrested 127 people in a six-month undercover operation against a Vietnamese-led crime syndicate accused of running loan-sharking rackets charging interest rates of up to 3,700 per cent, as well as illegal gambling and unlicensed bars in West Kowloon.
The syndicate is also alleged to have helped illegal immigrants find shelter and work, with police raiding eight premises on October 8 and 9.
Among those arrested were 10 alleged core members, including the suspected leader, a Vietnamese woman holding a Hong Kong identity card.

deduped_items.body_text:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi’s visit to South Korea on August 19-20, 2026, received relatively little international attention, despite being a consequential meeting for the Korean Peninsula. As China’s top diplomat and a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, Wang Yi delivered Beijing’s strategic foreign policy objectives toward the Korean Peninsula in an unusually candid way, not coded in diplomatic language.
Wang’s visit underscored China’s five closely connected foreign policy objectives. First, Beijing seeks to maintain permanent peace and stability on the Peninsula. Second, China categorically rejects North Korea’s nuclear weapons and maintains denuclearization as a long-term objective. Third, Beijing opposes the emergence of competing security blocs, whether a Russia-DPRK-China alignment or a consolidated U.S.-South Korea-Japan bloc. Fourth, China seeks to reduce U.S. military influence on the Peninsula and ultimately secure the removal of U.S. ground troops. Finally, China strives to build a regional security environment more conducive to its long-term objective of unification with Taiwan. These objectives appear not only in official statements but also in prominent publications from Chinese scholars.
First, North Korea’s belligerent behavior threatens peace and stability in the region. Missile launches and continued nuclear development provide justification for greater U.S-South Korea-Japan security cooperation and expanded military deployments in Northeast Asia. As Yijong Zheng states, “Beijing fundamentally opposes not merely North Korea’s possession of nuclear weapons, but the broader evolution of Northeast Asia’s security structure toward what may be called “deterrence normalization”: a situation in which North Korea’s nuclear status is increasingly accepted, while U.S. extended deterrence and regional military integration are continually reinforced.”[1]
Second, during his visit to Pyongyang on April 9-10, 2026, Wang Yi made it clear that North Korea’s belligerent behavior will come at a cost. As Zheng Jiyong argues, China “does not believe its nuclear status should be cost-free” and will use North Korea’s economic dependence to obtain “specific acts of restraint” from Pyongyang.[2] In exchange, Beijing will condition humanitarian assistance, access to border trade, energy supplies, infrastructure investment, and political backing on North Korean restraint. In practical terms, this means that further nuclear and missile provocations, military escalation, or actions that trigger expanded U.S., South Korean, and Japanese military deployments can come at the cost of diminished Chinese economic support and cooperation. Conversely, broader cooperation with Beijing requires Pyongyang to meet China’s requirements for “border stability, crisis communication, and military restraint.”
Third, China rejects bloc politics and the creation of Cold War-like architecture in Northeast Asia. The Russia-DPRK relationship contributes to a more divided security environment in Northeast Asia. Beijing categorically rejects joining a Russia-DPRK bloc[3] and does not want South Korea to become deeply integrated into a U.S.-Japan-South Korea military alliance. As Zheng Jiyong argues, “for Beijing, the biggest risk of closer North Korean-Russian cooperation is that it provides an excellent pretext for Japan, South Korea, and the U.S. to accelerate the integration of their bloc.” Encouraging South Korea to preserve its strategic autonomy and avoiding bloc confrontation are central to China’s objectives.
Moreover, China and South Korea share fundamental interests in peace, stability, and economic prosperity on the Korean Peninsula, while their economies remain deeply interconnected. During his visit, Wang called for the “resumption of a dialogue, and restoration of mutual trust” and for peaceful coexistence between South Korea and the DPRK, ultimately leading to lasting peace and stability.[4] In

deduped_items.title: Australia does not ‘need or want Russian fuel’, Chris Bowen says, after Trump deal to buy diesel from Putin

deduped_items.body_text:
Australia’s energy minister has said Russia “should not be rewarded for their illegal and immoral invasion of Ukraine” after the US president, Donald Trump, struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from the country.
The energy and climate change minister, Chris Bowen, said on Saturday Australia did not “need or want Russian fuel” while updating reporters on the country’s fuel reserves.
But One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said it was “important to work with countries, if we can have the resources we need”, not ruling out supporting Australia making such a deal of its own.
Trump wrote on social media on Saturday morning Australian time that after a “highly successful discussion” with Putin, Russia had agreed to immediately supply “300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel” to US and global markets, which would be followed by 500,000 tons in November rising later to 3m tons, depending on “the condition of [Russia’s] diesel refineries”.
The deal was criticised by Democrats and some Republicans. Trump is under political pressure due to high diesel prices in the US ahead of next month’s midterm elections.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said the deal “plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world”.
During a regular Saturday morning press conference to update Australians on the country’s fuel reserves, Bowen, who will lead negotiations at next month’s UN climate talks in Turkey, said: “We don’t need or want Russian fuel in Australia.”

Pauline Hanson has labelled Angus Taylor a “smarmy management consultant” and told attendees of a major conservative conference that they should not trust the Coalition, as the Liberal leader came under fire from hecklers in the crowd.
But Hanson has reiterated her offer to work together with the Coalition to defeat the Labor government, suggesting attendees of the annual Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) Australia in Brisbane put the Liberals or Nationals second on their ballot papers, behind One Nation.
Hanson’s insults aimed at the Coalition came moments after Taylor had given a mea culpa to the conference, criticising past Liberal governments – in which he was a key minister – for signing up to a net zero climate target, increasing immigration, and public spending during the pandemic.
“Your frustrations about where we let you down in the recent past are understandable and reasonable. Believe me, I share those frustrations,” the opposition leader said.
CPAC Australia heard from Taylor, Hanson and Nationals leader Matt Canavan on its opening morning on Saturday. It is the first time a sitting Liberal leader has addressed the event, and comes amid One Nation consistently outpolling the Coalition.
Hanson was the best received of all three conservative leaders, receiving a standing ovation from most of the crowd as she took the stage and an even more raucous applause as she finished. Taylor’s speech received a standing ovation from less than half the crowd.
While Taylor took a more conciliatory tone toward One Nation in his speech, Hanson’s address repeatedly slammed what she called the “uniparty”, referring to Labor and the Coalition.

Hanson told CPAC: “The uniparty have taken turns running this country into the ground. Both must be held accountable for the position they’ve put us in.”
She went on to point out the former Coalition government had made a commitment to net zero – a pledge since abolished by Taylor – and instituted the eSafety commissioner, both of which elicited boos from the audience.
“They [Liberals] signed us up to [net zero], so why would we trust them to get us out of it?” she said.
Hanson also said One Nation wanted a royal commission into net zero, including into “every decision the uniparty has made”.
But despite repeated criticism of the Coalition, Hanson said she was still keen for the conservative parties to cooperate.

deduped_items.title: Flydubai co-pilot began radicalisation in Australia, UAE prosecutors say
deduped_items.summary: Hammam al-Hammami’s shift towards extremism began while he was a student in Melbourne, according to Emirati attorney generalGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastThe co-pilot who tried to seize control of a flydubai jet flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week had been radicalised while studying in Australia, prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates said on Friday.Passengers and crew on the 30 September flight, which had 182 people onboard, intervened to stop 29-year-old Omani
deduped_items.body_text:
The co-pilot who tried to seize control of a flydubai jet flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week had been radicalised while studying in Australia, prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates said on Friday.
Passengers and crew on the 30 September flight, which had 182 people onboard, intervened to stop 29-year-old Omani national Hammam al-Hammami’s alleged attempt to hijack the plane on its way to Israel.
Dr Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, attorney general of the UAE, said al-Hammami’s shift towards extremism and terrorism began while he was studying at RMIT University in Melbourne.
During his time in Melbourne, he was influenced by the hardline takfiri ideology through reading extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks, the attorney general said.
The statement was shared on UAE government social media and first reported by the state-run Emirati news agency, known as WAM.
According to the statement, al-Hammami allegedly told prosecutors he adopted ideas advocating violence and terrorism and drew inspiration from the 9/11 terrorist attacks of 2001.
“The idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his thinking,” the statement said.
Al-Hammami allegedly prepared himself both psychologically and physically to carry out the alleged terror plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach.
Last weekend, Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged al-Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017.
On Monday, RMIT University confirmed that he had studied at its Melbourne campus, but “did not successfully complete an engineering qualification”.
Contacted by Guardian Australia on Saturday, RMIT said it did not have any further comment to make while an investigation led by the Victorian joint counter-terrorism team was ongoing.

deduped_items.title: He was ready to fight in the 'war on terror.' This post-9/11 veteran looks back at his decision to enlist
deduped_items.summary: After the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, CBC’s chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault reported on young people who enlisted to fight in the global "war on terror." Twenty-four years later, she tracked down one U.S. marine she met to find out if he got what he signed up for.
deduped_items.body_text:
Canada
He was ready to fight in the 'war on terror.' This post-9/11 veteran looks back at his decision to enlist
First interviewed by CBC News as a new recruit, Barry Sward recounts his war experience 24 years later
On Sept. 11, 2001, Barry Sward, a high school senior in Woodbridge, Va., watched the collapse of the twin towers on TV and knew he had made the right decision.
He had already enlisted to become a U.S. marine. Emboldened by a national tragedy, he now had an enemy to fight.
"There was a spike of revenge … and I did want to get the people that did this and hurt them really bad. I don't know why they're doing it," he told CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, who at the time was reporting on post-9/11 military recruitment.
In July 2002, he would start basic training at Parris Island, S.C., and just months later was part of the first units to enter Iraq as part of U.S. President George W. Bush's so-called "war on terror."
After Sept. 11, 2001, U.S. veterans are about twice as likely as those who signed up before them to have served in a combat zone, according to a 2019 Pew Research survey that polled 1,284 veterans. As a result, they are more likely to have been scarred by the battle wounds of war — not only physically, but mentally, too.
In that same survey, half of the respondents said they had emotionally traumatic or distressing experiences, yet only a third sought help to deal with what they faced.
CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, left, sits with U.S. marine vetreran Barry Sward, who shares photos and mementoes he saved from his time serving in Iraq in 2003, including a half pack of cigarettes, cassettes and his service cap. (Roxanna Woloshyn/CBC News)
In August of this year, Arsenault tracked down an almost unrecognizable Sward in Falmouth, Va., 24 years after their first interview.
She asked him: "Are you the same person you were when you went in?"
"No, definitely not," said Sward, now facing the effects of that deployment to Iraq — a resulting back injury and a PTSD diagnosis.
The post-9/11 patriotic recruits
In the days and months after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, media reports described long lines at military recruitment offices made up of young people who wanted to fight for their country.
"Post-9/11, you have a burst of patriotism and a need to serve, and there are plenty of stories of people who immediately left their jobs, went down to a recruiting station, or finally decided that they were gonna join," said Jason Dempsey, a scholar of American civil military relations at Columbia University.
"But that was not the majority of folks entering service. And in the grand scheme of things was a very temporary blip."
Sward, seen here in 2002, participated in basic training at Parris Island, S.C., as part of his preparations in the U.S. marine corps beginning in July 2002. (CBC News)
Numbers provided by the four primary branches of the military don't show a dramatic rise in enlistment immediately following Sept. 11 compared to other years.
Dempsey said the most common reasons for someone to join the military is a history of service in their families, a desire for financial security or educational opportunities and enlisting during a period of high unemployment.
Regardless of their reason for signing up, that generation of post-9/11 fighters would go on to participate in long-lasting wars in Afghanistan and Iraq — the latter of which saw U.S. foces officially withdraw just last month.
Serving in Iraq was 'frustrating'
In March 2003, as part of the global war on terror, U.S. President Bush announced forces would be invading Iraq if then-president Saddam Hussein did not leave.
Days later, Sward's unit, the 2nd Battalion, 8th Marines, crossed into the country. Their mission was to secure bridges in a highly defended enemy territory so troops could ultimately make their way to Baghdad.
March 23, 2003, is a day that haunts Sward. It was the beginning of a deadly fight known as the Battle o

deduped_items.summary: After the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, CBC’s chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault reported on young people who enlisted to fight in the global "war on terror." Twenty-four years later, she tracked down one U.S. marine she met to find out if he got what he signed up for.

He was ready to fight in the 'war on terror.' This post-9/11 veteran looks back at his decision to enlist
First interviewed by CBC News as a new recruit, Barry Sward recounts his war experience 24 years later
On Sept. 11, 2001, Barry Sward, a high school senior in Woodbridge, Va., watched the collapse of the twin towers on TV and knew he had made the right decision.
He had already enlisted to become a U.S. marine. Emboldened by a national tragedy, he now had an enemy to fight.
"There was a spike of revenge … and I did want to get the people that did this and hurt them really bad. I don't know why they're doing it," he told CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, who at the time was reporting on post-9/11 military recruitment.
In July 2002, he would start basic training at Parris Island, S.C., and just months later was part of the first units to enter Iraq as part of U.S. President George W. Bush's so-called "war on terror."
After Sept. 11, 2001, U.S. veterans are about twice as likely as those who signed up before them to have served in a combat zone, according to a 2019 Pew Research survey that polled 1,284 veterans. As a result, they are more likely to have been scarred by the battle wounds of war — not only physically, but mentally, too.
In that same survey, half of the respondents said they had emotionally traumatic or distressing experiences, yet only a third sought help to deal with what they faced.
CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, left, sits with U.S. marine vetreran Barry Sward, who shares photos and mementoes he saved from his time serving in Iraq in 2003, including a half pack of cigarettes, cassettes and his service cap. (Roxanna Woloshyn/CBC News)
In August of this year, Arsenault tracked down an almost unrecognizable Sward in Falmouth, Va., 24 years after their first interview.
She asked him: "Are you the same person you were when you went in?"
"No, definitely not," said Sward, now facing the effects of that deployment to Iraq — a resulting back injury and a PTSD diagnosis.
The post-9/11 patriotic recruits
In the days and months after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, media reports described long lines at military recruitment offices made up of young people who wanted to fight for their country.
"Post-9/11, you have a burst of patriotism and a need to serve, and there are plenty of stories of people who immediately left their jobs, went down to a recruiting station, or finally decided that they were gonna join," said Jason Dempsey, a scholar of American civil military relations at Columbia University.
"But that was not the majority of folks entering service. And in the grand scheme of things was a very temporary blip."
Sward, seen here in 2002, participated in basic training at Parris Island, S.C., as part of his preparations in the U.S. marine corps beginning in July 2002. (CBC News)
Numbers provided by the four primary branches of the military don't show a dramatic rise in enlistment immediately following Sept. 11 compared to other years.
Dempsey said the most common reasons for someone to join the military is a history of service in their families, a desire for financial security or educational opportunities and enlisting during a period of high unemployment.
Regardless of their reason for signing up, that generation of post-9/11 fighters would go on to participate in long-lasting wars in Afghanistan and Iraq — the latter of which saw U.S. foces officially withdraw just last month.
Serving in Iraq was 'frustrating'
In March 2003, as part of the global war on terror, U.S. President Bush announced forces would be invading Iraq if then-president Saddam Hussein did not leave.
Days later, Sward's unit, the 2nd Battalion, 8th Marines, crossed into the country. Their mission was to secure bridges in a highly defended enemy territory so troops could ultimately make their way to Baghdad.

He was ready to fight in the 'war on terror.' This post-9/11 veteran looks back at his decision to enlist
First interviewed by CBC News as a new recruit, Barry Sward recounts his war experience 24 years later
On Sept. 11, 2001, Barry Sward, a high school senior in Woodbridge, Va., watched the collapse of the twin towers on TV and knew he had made the right decision.
He had already enlisted to become a U.S. marine. Emboldened by a national tragedy, he now had an enemy to fight.
"There was a spike of revenge … and I did want to get the people that did this and hurt them really bad. I don't know why they're doing it," he told CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, who at the time was reporting on post-9/11 military recruitment.
In July 2002, he would start basic training at Parris Island, S.C., and just months later was part of the first units to enter Iraq as part of U.S. President George W. Bush's so-called "war on terror."
After Sept. 11, 2001, U.S. veterans are about twice as likely as those who signed up before them to have served in a combat zone, according to a 2019 Pew Research survey that polled 1,284 veterans. As a result, they are more likely to have been scarred by the battle wounds of war — not only physically, but mentally, too.
In that same survey, half of the respondents said they had emotionally traumatic or distressing experiences, yet only a third sought help to deal with what they faced.
CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, left, sits with U.S. marine vetreran Barry Sward, who shares photos and mementoes he saved from his time serving in Iraq in 2003, including a half pack of cigarettes, cassettes and his service cap. (Roxanna Woloshyn/CBC News)
In August of this year, Arsenault tracked down an almost unrecognizable Sward in Falmouth, Va., 24 years after their first interview.
She asked him: "Are you the same person you were when you went in?"
"No, definitely not," said Sward, now facing the effects of that deployment to Iraq — a resulting back injury and a PTSD diagnosis.
The post-9/11 patriotic recruits
In the days and months after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, media reports described long lines at military recruitment offices made up of young people who wanted to fight for their country.
"Post-9/11, you have a burst of patriotism and a need to serve, and there are plenty of stories of people who immediately left their jobs, went down to a recruiting station, or finally decided that they were gonna join," said Jason Dempsey, a scholar of American civil military relations at Columbia University.
"But that was not the majority of folks entering service. And in the grand scheme of things was a very temporary blip."
Sward, seen here in 2002, participated in basic training at Parris Island, S.C., as part of his preparations in the U.S. marine corps beginning in July 2002. (CBC News)
Numbers provided by the four primary branches of the military don't show a dramatic rise in enlistment immediately following Sept. 11 compared to other years.
Dempsey said the most common reasons for someone to join the military is a history of service in their families, a desire for financial security or educational opportunities and enlisting during a period of high unemployment.
Regardless of their reason for signing up, that generation of post-9/11 fighters would go on to participate in long-lasting wars in Afghanistan and Iraq — the latter of which saw U.S. foces officially withdraw just last month.
Serving in Iraq was 'frustrating'
In March 2003, as part of the global war on terror, U.S. President Bush announced forces would be invading Iraq if then-president Saddam Hussein did not leave.
Days later, Sward's unit, the 2nd Battalion, 8th Marines, crossed into the country. Their mission was to secure bridges in a highly defended enemy territory so troops could ultimately make their way to Baghdad.
March 23, 2003, is a day that haunts Sward. It was the beginning of a deadly fight known as the Battle o

deduped_items.title: Isaías se debilita pero sigue amenazando con inundaciones mientras miles se quedan sin electricidad
deduped_items.summary: Isaías, ahora ciclón postropical, avanza por Alabama tras tocar tierra como huracán. Persisten riesgos de tornados e inundaciones en el sureste de EE.UU.Más de 911.000 usuarios quedaron sin electricidad. Las fuertes lluvias y marejadas continúan afectando el Panhandle y partes de Georgia.
deduped_items.body_text:
GULF BREEZE, Florida, EE.UU. (AP) — Isaías perdió la categoría de huracán durante la noche, pero las amenazas de inundaciones repentinas y la posibilidad de tornados persistían el sábado mientras avanzaba tierra adentro a través de Alabama.
La tormenta, ahora convertida en ciclón postropical, tocó tierra el viernes como huracán de categoría 2 y avanzó rápidamente hacia el norte a través de Alabama, mientras la potencia de sus vientos disminuía drásticamente a apenas 55 kilómetros/hora (35 mph). Pero la posibilidad de marejadas ciclónicas potencialmente mortales seguía activa en algunas zonas de la franja noroccidental de Florida, conocida como el Panhandle. Además, durante el fin de semana podrían registrarse acumulaciones de entre 10 y 20 centímetros (4 a 8 pulgadas) de lluvia en el sur de Alabama, el Panhandle y el Big Bend de Florida.
Isaías se encontraba a unos 40 kilómetros (25 millas) al sur-suroeste de Montgomery, Alabama, y a casi 170 kilómetros (105 millas) al sur de Birmingham, Alabama, con vientos máximos sostenidos de 55 kilómetros/hora (35 mph), informó el sábado el Centro Nacional de Huracanes (NHC, por sus siglas en inglés). Se espera que se desplace hacia el valle de Tennessee más tarde el sábado y el domingo.
Se han levantado todas las alertas por tormenta tropical y marejada ciclónica, pero los meteorólogos advirtieron que las condiciones podrían favorecer la formación de tornados en el Panhandle, Georgia y las Carolinas.
Isaías llegó a las inmediaciones de Destin, Florida, como el primer huracán de la temporada del Atlántico. Los vientos huracanados azotaron un tramo de la costa del golfo conocido por sus playas de arena blanca y fina salpicada de casas vacacionales, bares frente al mar y puestos de mariscos.
“La tormenta ya está aquí. Abróchense los cinturones en este momento. No salgan a las calles”, dijo el gobernador de Florida, Ron DeSantis, en una conferencia de prensa el viernes.
Las carreteras en Destin estaban inundadas, mientras que en la cercana Pensacola, la policía advirtió a los residentes que se mantuvieran alejados de los viales debido a la presencia de escombros en la calzada. Aunque por el momento no se conoce el alcance de los daños, muchos residentes publicaron en internet fotos de árboles y líneas eléctricas caídas, y un video en redes sociales mostró cómo era arrancado el techo de una posada en Pensacola.
Algunos condados del Panhandle suspendieron temporalmente la respuesta de emergencia el viernes por la noche debido a las peligrosas condiciones.
Partes del sur de Alabama también estaban inundadas, y las autoridades en Mobile informaron de árboles y líneas eléctricas caídos. Las carreteras en el condado de Houston, en la esquina sureste del estado, quedaron cerradas debido a condiciones similares.
En Florida, Alabama y Georgia, más de 911.000 clientes estaban sin electricidad a primera hora del sábado, según poweroutage.com.
Tim Mowry, que capeó la tormenta desde su casa en Pensacola, contó que el viento era tan intenso que sonaba como el silbato de un tren al colarse por una rendija en la puerta de su patio. Se quedó sin electricidad alrededor de las 4:30 de la tarde, pero contaba con un generador. También tenía agua estancada en su patio trasero y parte de la cerca de su propiedad fue arrancada. Pero, en general, dijo que la tormenta no fue tan mala como esperaba.
“En lo que respecta a Pensacola, realmente tuvimos suerte”, apuntó Mowry.
Su hijo, que vive a unos 15 minutos, intentó conducir hasta su casa después de quedarse sin electricidad, pero tuvo que dar la vuelta porque árboles y líneas eléctricas caídas bloqueaban las carreteras, contó.
Isaías fue el primer huracán que azota el este de Estados Unidos desde el paso de Milton por la costa del golfo en Florida en 2024. Se prevé que descargue fuertes lluvias y cause posibles inundaciones en gran parte del sureste durante el fin de semana, y luego en partes la región centro-norte y el noreste del país hasta el lunes.

Lo primero lo inspiran Lionel Messi y el equipo –jugadores y cuerpo técnico- que lo acompañó durante su etapa más gloriosa en la Selección, de la que se despidió el martes con un partido olvidable y una ceremonia mal organizada a la que salvó el sentimiento de gratitud que iba y venía de la cancha a las tribunas. La vergüenza corre por cuenta de la conducción de la AFA, con Claudio Tapia y Pablo

deduped_items.title: El beso de la mujer araña: A 50 años del encuentro con la novela emblema de Manuel Puig
deduped_items.summary: La historia del encierro en una prisión política del militante Valentín Arregui y la ‘loca’ Luis Molina en aquellos años de idealismo y convulsión marcó una nueva consagración para el escritor argentino Manuel Puig. Es cierto que su pluma ya había dejado entrever su amor por el cine, sus fantasías tempranas con las divas y los monstruos de Hollywood, y que su obra había cosechado el éxito local con Boquitas pintadas a fines de los cincuenta, y el exilio marcaba el pulso de la mirada a distancia.

deduped_items.title: Is the Spanish Transition a Model for Venezuela?
deduped_items.summary: Spain's democratization yielded a stable party system and longstanding agreements, but didn’t address the past. Should we follow its steps?
deduped_items.body_text:
Is the Spanish Transition a Model for Venezuela?
Spain's democratization yielded a stable party system and longstanding agreements, but didn’t address the past. Should we follow its steps?
King Juan Carlos I summons party leaders after the failed 1981 coup. From left to right: Santiago Carrillo (Communist Party), Agustín Rodríguez Sahagún (Defence Minister), Adolfo Suárez (Prime Minister), Juan Carlos I, Felipe González (PSOE) and Manuel Fraga (People’s Alliance, later PP).
(“Gosh, no! Not another hyper-comparative article about two distant political conflicts…” Apologies. We’ll try to make it a fun read).
More often than not, our intellectual circles have felt tempted to look at alien historical episodes in a never-ending search for resolute answers that shed light on our present. In 2023, when Maduro flirted with attacking US-supported Guyana, some revisited the Falklands War as a sign that a serious military incursion would be a fatal mistake that would lead to the dictatorship’s downfall. Then came the road to the 2024 presidential election; many feared (rightfully, in the end) that the country would plunge into the “Nicaragua scenario” if the dictator refused to recognize his defeat. Others momentarily wondered if enough external pressure could give way to a Guatemala-style transfer of power and a weak transition government.
The days of terror seem to be behind us, yet there’s no progressive reformer like Raúl Alfonsín steering the wheel of justice. Instead, Donald Trump gave us the Pizza Hut scenario. Here, Delcy Rodríguez has become the poster girl of the MAGA international franchise. Here, too, US geopolitical ambitions and business interests at times seem to be competing with the need for free elections and a democratic regime.
Is Rodríguez our Mikhail Gorbachev, trying to open the economy and political system just enough while attempting to save the chavista State from outright collapse? What if chavismo is already dead and she’s the Yeltsin of the Caribbean, the feeble leader who will give away the country’s riches to oligarchs in an arbitrary fashion, laying the ground for a new form of autocracy?
Or might Delcy be the chavista version of Adolfo Suárez, the not-so-brilliant and obscure but highly charismatic Francoist insider? Suárez finished the job after a remarkable run, surviving a period of meagre political support, declining approval rates and a coup d’etat that could have killed him. The comparison now sounds like an insult to the Spaniard. Like Gorbachev in today’s Russia, Suárez has become a sort of mythical statesman abroad while Spanish right- and left-wing critics dispute his legacy.
There are genuine similarities between the process currently unfolding in Caracas and the outset of Spain’s democracy, as well as room for gross contrasts. While 2026 has been insane for Venezuelans, Spain exactly fifty years ago was astonishing due to the speed at which Suárez acted in unilaterally dismantling the regime from within the regime. The dictator was finally gone, and as soon as he had the chance, the new King ordered a politician without strong ideological convictions to establish a full parliamentary democracy.
Suárez took office in June 1976. The Law for Political Reform, meant to pave the way for a new democratic legislature (with the King acting as a key enforcer), was through six months later. Spain held general elections within a year. That was just the start. What followed was a sequence full of the raw materials that tend to feed these history-making episodes: secret meetings and grand bargains between rivals and strange bedfellows, journalists acting like hinges, political violence, and leaders who soon become overwhelmed by their own decisions and actions.
How the transition worked out
When scholars praise the atmosphere of consensus that defined Spain in the 1970s, they generally speak of the close cooperation between regime reformers and opposition moderates in devising broad agreements that fastene

What if chavismo is already dead and she’s the Yeltsin of the Caribbean, the feeble leader who will give away the country’s riches to oligarchs in an arbitrary fashion, laying the ground for a new form of autocracy?
Or might Delcy be the chavista version of Adolfo Suárez, the not-so-brilliant and obscure but highly charismatic Francoist insider? Suárez finished the job after a remarkable run, surviving a period of meagre political support, declining approval rates and a coup d’etat that could have killed him. The comparison now sounds like an insult to the Spaniard. Like Gorbachev in today’s Russia, Suárez has become a sort of mythical statesman abroad while Spanish right- and left-wing critics dispute his legacy.
There are genuine similarities between the process currently unfolding in Caracas and the outset of Spain’s democracy, as well as room for gross contrasts. While 2026 has been insane for Venezuelans, Spain exactly fifty years ago was astonishing due to the speed at which Suárez acted in unilaterally dismantling the regime from within the regime. The dictator was finally gone, and as soon as he had the chance, the new King ordered a politician without strong ideological convictions to establish a full parliamentary democracy.
Suárez took office in June 1976. The Law for Political Reform, meant to pave the way for a new democratic legislature (with the King acting as a key enforcer), was through six months later. Spain held general elections within a year. That was just the start. What followed was a sequence full of the raw materials that tend to feed these history-making episodes: secret meetings and grand bargains between rivals and strange bedfellows, journalists acting like hinges, political violence, and leaders who soon become overwhelmed by their own decisions and actions.

deduped_items.summary: After a three-year absence, Anrich Nortje’s pace helped reduce the visitors to 124-6, but Pat Cummins and Matt Renshaw fought back with an unbeaten 63-run stand in first innings of first Test before bad light stopped play. South Africa will be hoping to pick off the rest of the Aussie batting line-up when play resumes on Saturday. At close of play, Australia, who elected to bat first, were 187-6 (Matt Renshaw 46*, Pat Cummins 33*, Wiaan Mulder 2-31, Anrich Nortje 2-40).

deduped_items.title: Mozambique's Graca Machel among 21st-Century's 'Top of The Top-10 Merit Sovereigns'
deduped_items.summary: 21st-Century's Top of the Top-10 Merit Sovereigns Hierarchy Crowns Graca Machel alongside Stephen Soldz, King Charles III, Francesca Albanese, Polymath Aurangzeb Hafi and Greta Thunberg among others.
deduped_items.body_text:
Audio By Vocalize
Graca Machel of Mozambique has emerged as one of the era-defining standout names in a sweeping new global merit ranking, cited twice over for her decades of work on behalf of children caught in armed conflict, as Impact Hallmarks (IH©) unveiled its list of the ‘Sovereign Merit Icons of the 21st Century’.
The Britain-based cross-disciplinary indexing system names 38 individuals across humanitarian work, science, athletics, monarchy and youth activism, scored against a 1,000-point framework that its authors say was designed to reward documented achievement over public visibility.
Machel, credited as architect of a landmark United Nations report assessing the impact of armed conflict on children over a 25-year span, scored more than 940 points to place second in the Humanitarianism and Social Justice category, a distinction she shares with Francesca Albanese, the UN Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories, recognised for her 2024 report ‘Anatomy of Genocide’ and for facing sanctions over her work.
She appears a second time in the Icons of Dignified Asceticism category, alongside former Finnish president Tarja Halonen and former New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern, each scoring above 910 points, and is named a third time among the Quarticentennial Merit Vanguards, a tier recognising researchers who provided evidentiary baselines for major UN constitutive documentation.
Topping the Humanitarianism and Social Justice category outright is Stephen Soldz of the United States, who scored 967 points for what assessors called his monumental documentation of psychologically coercive interrogation tactics used against war prisoners — work IH© described as the first academic condemnation of using sacred religious texts as instruments of torture, and which the assessors named the ‘Magna Carta’ of ethics and human inviolability.
Also recognised is Greta Thunberg of Sweden, indexed in two separate categories: third place in Resilience, Endurance and Nature-Centricity with 933 points, for an arc running from her solitary school-strike movement to leading high-risk flotilla missions carrying aid toward Gaza, including the Freedom Flotilla in June 2025 and the 44-nation Global Sumud Flotilla in September 2025, whose interception led to the detention of 450 activists and sparked protests across three continents, and again in the Young Trailblazing Icons category with 920 points.
In the Scientific Endeavours category, physicist Dr Fritjof Capra of the United States shares first place with Arch-Polymath Sir Aurangzeb of Pakistan with 950+ points for both.
Dr Capra is credited for his systems theory of life and for framing a composite worldview against the Newtonian-Cartesian mechanistic paradigm.
Prof Aurangzeb Hafi is recognised for integrating the ‘scientific pentarchy’, for identifying the mega-toxification of underground water reserves, which is linked to prevailing sewage-drainage practices in developing countries, for presenting the first ‘Deca-Archic Phygital Literacy Model’, and for the discovery of Magneto-Hydro-Tropism (MHT).
Prof Hafi is named in three separate categories overall, also placing in Paradigm-Trailblazing Icons with 910 points and second in Multiple Iconicities with 957 points, cited for research spanning 93 subject fields.
King Charles III of the United Kingdom is named in the Paradigm-Trailblazing Icons category with 930 points, cited as a decades-long advocate for world peace, interfaith harmony and global ecology, now serving as head of state of multiple nations.
Pope Francis leads the Resilience, Endurance and Nature-Centricity category with 940 points, and James Harrison of Australia, the ‘’Man with the Golden Arm’, tops the Multiple Iconicities category for blood-plasma donations credited with saving roughly 2.4 million lives.
Both figures were living iconicity-participants during the retrospective evaluation timeline (2000–2025), but are deceased at the time of the gazette's o

deduped_items.title: Mozambique's Graca Machel among 21st-Century's 'Top of The Top-10 Merit Sovereigns'
deduped_items.summary: 21st-Century's Top of the Top-10 Merit Sovereigns Hierarchy Crowns Graca Machel alongside Stephen Soldz, King Charles III, Francesca Albanese, Polymath Aurangzeb Hafi and Greta Thunberg among others.
deduped_items.body_text:
Audio By Vocalize
Graca Machel of Mozambique has emerged as one of the era-defining standout names in a sweeping new global merit ranking, cited twice over for her decades of work on behalf of children caught in armed conflict, as Impact Hallmarks (IH©) unveiled its list of the ‘Sovereign Merit Icons of the 21st Century’.
The Britain-based cross-disciplinary indexing system names 38 individuals across humanitarian work, science, athletics, monarchy and youth activism, scored against a 1,000-point framework that its authors say was designed to reward documented achievement over public visibility.
Machel, credited as architect of a landmark United Nations report assessing the impact of armed conflict on children over a 25-year span, scored more than 940 points to place second in the Humanitarianism and Social Justice category, a distinction she shares with Francesca Albanese, the UN Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories, recognised for her 2024 report ‘Anatomy of Genocide’ and for facing sanctions over her work.
She appears a second time in the Icons of Dignified Asceticism category, alongside former Finnish president Tarja Halonen and former New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern, each scoring above 910 points, and is named a third time among the Quarticentennial Merit Vanguards, a tier recognising researchers who provided evidentiary baselines for major UN constitutive documentation.
Topping the Humanitarianism and Social Justice category outright is Stephen Soldz of the United States, who scored 967 points for what assessors called his monumental documentation of psychologically coercive interrogation tactics used against war prisoners — work IH© described as the first academic condemnation of using sacred religious texts as instruments of torture, and which the assessors named the ‘Magna Carta’ of ethics and human inviolability.
Also recognised is Greta Thunberg of Sweden, indexed in two separate categories: third place in Resilience, Endurance and Nature-Centricity with 933 points, for an arc running from her solitary school-strike movement to leading high-risk flotilla missions carrying aid toward Gaza, including the Freedom Flotilla in June 2025 and the 44-nation Global Sumud Flotilla in September 2025, whose interception led to the detention of 450 activists and sparked protests across three continents, and again in the Young Trailblazing Icons category with 920 points.
In the Scientific Endeavours category, physicist Dr Fritjof Capra of the United States shares first place with Arch-Polymath Sir Aurangzeb of Pakistan with 950+ points for both.
Dr Capra is credited for his systems theory of life and for framing a composite worldview against the Newtonian-Cartesian mechanistic paradigm.
Prof Aurangzeb Hafi is recognised for integrating the ‘scientific pentarchy’, for identifying the mega-toxification of underground water reserves, which is linked to prevailing sewage-drainage practices in developing countries, for presenting the first ‘Deca-Archic Phygital Literacy Model’, and for the discovery of Magneto-Hydro-Tropism (MHT).
Prof Hafi is named in three separate categories overall, also placing in Paradigm-Trailblazing Icons with 910 points and second in Multiple Iconicities with 957 points, cited for research spanning 93 subject fields.
King Charles III of the United Kingdom is named in the Paradigm-Trailblazing Icons category with 930 points, cited as a decades-long advocate for world peace, interfaith harmony and global ecology, now serving as head of state of multiple nations.
Pope Francis leads the Resilience, Endurance and Nature-Centricity category with 940 points, and James Harrison of Australia, the ‘’Man with the Golden Arm’, tops the Multiple Iconicities category for blood-plasma donations credited with saving roughly 2.4 million lives.

deduped_items.title: Rapport de HRW sur l'Ouganda: les États-Unis se servent de l'accord pour annuler les demandes d'asile
deduped_items.summary: Depuis janvier 2025, les États-Unis ont annulé plus de 2 700 procédures d’asile sans même examiner les demandes sur le fond. Le motif : ces personnes - pour la plupart africaines - pourraient solliciter une protection en Ouganda, en vertu d’un accord conclu en juillet 2025 entre Washington et Kampala. C’est l’une des conséquences de la politique d’expulsions vers des pays africains mise en place par l’administration Trump, et dénoncée dans un rapport de Human Rights Watch publié le 8 octobre. Po

deduped_items.summary: Trois jours après leur retour à Kidal, les soldats maliens et leurs partenaires russes de l'Africa Corps sécurisent la ville et ses alentours. L'armée mène quotidiennement des frappes aériennes dans la région mais n'a pas encore poursuivi sa progression au sol. This is an entry from: Live: Yemeni government says 1,400 Houthis killed in 2,750 strikes
Sanaa airport hit by four air strikes, large blast heard at Riyadh airport
10 October 2026 14:19 BST
Yemen's Sanaa International Airport has been hit by four air strikes, Houthi-affiliated media is reporting, after forces loyal to Yemen’s Saudi-backed government announced they have been carrying out air strikes across Houthi-held areas.
The same media also reported three air strikes targeting communications networks in Al-Muhabsha city.
Meanwhile, Reuters reported that a loud blast was heard from Saudi Arabia's Riyadh Airport, citing eyewitnesses and people familiar with the matter.
No immediate comment was made from Saudi Arabian authorities on any incident at the airport.

Eight Palestinians killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza during anniversary of US-brokered 'ceasefire'
10 October 2026 13:55 BST
Al Jazeera has reported that at least eight Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces in several areas of the Gaza Strip since dawn on Saturday, including an eight-year-old Palestinian girl.
The deaths come on the first anniversary of a US-brokered "ceasefire" in Gaza, during which more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in ongoing Israeli attacks.
The Israeli military has also continued to carry out several raids across southern Lebanon on Saturday, according to the country’s official National News Agency (NNA), targeting the Jarmaq area and the towns of al-Mansouri and Wadi Zibqin with air strikes and shelling.

Police estimated that 30,000 people took part in the demonstration, organised by trade unions amid growing opposition to austerity measures.

deduped_items.body_text:
Enemies of Convenience: Ethiopia’s New Opposition Alignment and the Question of What Comes Next
On September 20, 2026, seven Ethiopian armed and political movements announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Coalition for Survival, declaring that they sought to remove the Prosperity Party-led government and establish an inclusive transitional government. The announcement was followed by a major TPLF offensive on September 23 across Tigray, Amhara and Afar. Federal and allied forces have since regained ground, including Mekelle’s airport, which government-aligned forces said they had retaken on October 3. The fighting is the most serious escalation since the 2020–2022 war.
The coalition’s announced membership included the Amhara Fano National Movement, Oromo Liberation Army, Tigray People’s Liberation Front, Ogaden National Liberation Front, an Afar armed group, Benishangul Peoples’ Liberation Movement and Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movement. But within days, GPDM and ONLF publicly denied joining. That matters: even the coalition’s composition is contested.
Former Adversaries, Conflicting Objectives
The three most consequential armed actors are the TPLF, Fano and OLA. Their histories and political objectives are sharply different. Shared opposition to Addis Ababa does not erase those differences.
Ethiopian politics has repeatedly produced alliances of convenience. TPLF and OLF were once partners in the 1991 transition, but the TPLF pushed the OLF out in 1993. The OLF was later outlawed, while thousands of suspectedsupporters were detained or killed during successive security campaigns. When the OLF returned from exile after Abiy came to power, it entered politics as a legal party, but armed factions continued fighting as the OLA.
The contradiction with Fano is even deeper. Fano presents the post-1991 political order and ethnic federalism as a source of Ethiopia’s fragmentation and as an arrangement hostile to Amhara interests. The OLA, by contrast, continues to pursue an Oromo nationalist project, with prominent OLA figures publicly describing independence as an objective. Fano and Oromo armed movements have also accused each other of atrocities and territorial aggression. These are not minor disagreements that can simply be postponed until after victory.
From Wartime Enemies to Unlikely Allies
The most striking feature of the new alignment is the relationship between the TPLF, Fano and Eritrea. During the 2020–2022 Tigray war, Eritrean forces and Fano fought alongside the federal government against the TPLF. The Pretoria Peace Agreement ended that war in November 2022, but Eritrea and Fano were not parties to the agreement. Though some analysts have argued that their exclusion left important grievances unresolved, the deeper source of their discontent was their belief that they were in a position not only to defeat the TPLF but potentially to eliminate it as a military and political force, and that the federal government had effectively rescued the TPLF by agreeing to the peace deal.
The agreement also created a new dispute between the TPLF and Addis Ababa over disarmament, territory and the administration of Tigray. The TPLF’s subsequent struggle with the federal government in violation of the Pretoria peace agreement contributed to a deeper political and military split inside Tigray. Tigrayan fighters dissatisfied with the TPLF’s course broke away in 2025 and formed the Tigray Peace Force, which has received apparent support from federal authorities. The TPF has since fought alongside federal forces against TPLF forces.
This history makes the current alignment remarkable. Former battlefield enemies are now cooperating against the government they once fought alongside or, in the TPLF’s case, fought against.

deduped_items.body_text:
Ethiopia’s volatile politics: the June 2026 parliamentary elections, the National Dialogue, and violent conflict
In a surprise to absolutely no one, Ethiopia’s ruling Prosperity Party (PP) led by PM Abiy Ahmed won the 1 June 2026 parliamentary elections in a landslide. The outcome has evoked few commentaries in the global media or even in Ethiopia itself. There was a c. 90% win of parliamentary seats for the PP. This is, like in previous elections (2021, or 2015), a kind of Communist country result. It indeed was a well-organised operation, a classic case of what in Ethiopia since the Derg-regime (1974-1991) is called an “organisational operation” (Amharic: dirigitawi sera). That may be regretted or lauded but reflects political reality. Ethiopia still has no deep-rooted democratic political culture, certainly not on the national level: there was always violent competition for power and lack of freedoms, and people mostly went to the polls because of a mixture of duty, pride, and fear.
At around the same time, in August, some results of the ‘National Dialogue’ process were announced – a nation-wide ambitious consultation initiated in 2022 and closed off after a conference (15 July-22 August), and they may prove to be more important than the elections as such. The yet unpublished full recommendations of this unique although not perfect Dialogue were offered to the federal government on 3 October and will have to be addressed by the newly elected parliament. Interesting in the discussions and the recommendations was a growing ambivalence about ‘ethnic politics’.
First about the June elections. What did they show? Technically efficient, they were a repeat of the process of elite consolidation: the incumbent can continue as usual. The security situation also prevented voting in at least 143 polling stations in 46 constituencies. Since early September we also saw an escalation of violent strife, especially in Tigray, Amhara, and Oromia Regions, and the national political arena seems to further fragment: clearly, the elections did not have a stabilising effect.
What few people talk about is the electoral system that facilitates the return of the incumbent party, time and again. Ethiopia does not have proportional representation but a district system, with a ‘first past the post’ mechanism (created by the previous, EPRDF regime). It means that the more parties participate (there were 48 registered parties..), the more the chances are that the most powerful and influential party – of course the one in power, i.e., the PP – will reach the threshold first, even if it has, say, only 15% of the votes in the voting district. In addition, there is a, to many analysts, unhealthy preponderance of ethnic-based parties: a divisive element in any election system, leading to uncritical, loyalty block-voting rather than a focus on issue politics and coalitions or on evaluating the concrete results and human impact of policies. My argument is that this ‘district system’ and the ethno-federal formula mean that the incumbent cannot lose. This hinders effective democratic representation. In an alternative system, however, ‘ethnic’ parties should be discouraged, because that would, under current conditions of elite politics’, de facto continue the ethnic block voting. Realistically, however, this will not happen soon, and thus, political quagmire and conflicts will continue.
With PP hegemony in parliament confirmed and only a marginal role for opposition parties or civil-society forces, the question is if pressing national concerns will be tackled in a new way. These include the (effects of) ongoing armed conflicts, the large number of IDPs, regionally unbalanced developmental policies, the weak justice system, and the perpetual economic problems. deduped_items.body_text:
How Zambia Defeated an Election Petition Without Ever Arguing the Case
Zambia’s 13 August general election was already fraught before anyone tried to challenge its result, according to an account human rights lawyer Linda Kasonde has since published on her Substack. The army had been deployed to polling stations, she writes, a role outside its constitutional mandate. The Electoral Commission suspended vote tallying for six hours over reports of attacks on polling agents, during which only police and soldiers had access to the ballots. Opposition candidate Brian Mundubile’s home was raided and eleven of his associates were abducted. Former Cabinet Minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was fatally shot in the same raid. Authorities denied the killing for five days, until a habeas corpus application forced them to confirm it. Hakainde Hichilema was declared the winner on 18 August with around 61 percent against Mundubile’s 38 percent, though the Christian Churches Monitoring Group’s own assessment of its parallel vote tabulation had projected a closer 56 percent.
It is against that backdrop that Linda Kasonde decided to petition the result. Kasonde is a human rights lawyer and former president of the Law Association of Zambia. She petitioned under Article 103(1)(b) of the Constitution, which allows any citizen to challenge an election on the ground that it was not free and fair. She had seven days from the declaration to file, under Article 101(4). She did not get seven days. On 24 August, a day before her deadline, the government shut down the courts. The closures covered the Constitutional Court, the Supreme Court, the High Court in Lusaka, and premises in Ndola, Chipata and Livingstone. The stated reason was unspecified security concerns. Police later described the closuresas nationwide security risk assessments at government premises, without saying what threat had prompted them. The closure lasted until 27 August. In an essay she has since published on her Substack, Kasonde describes what she did next.
In her account, she writes that she had tried to file electronically before, under new e-filing rules introduced in May 2026, and had been told the rules were not yet operational. With the courthouses sealed, she tried again anyway, emailing her petition to the Chief Registrar’s official address. The judiciary’s website, she says she was told, had been disabled. So she sent the documents to Chief Justice Mumba Malila’s personal email instead, explaining that the shutdown had left her no other option. A day later, Kasonde recounts, the judiciary’s public relations office confirmed receipt, and the Chief Justice himself said that while the method was “highly irregular,” he would forward the documents to the Constitutional Court. Kasonde describes the relief as short-lived. A separate statement soon followed from the Chief Administrator, asserting that no petition had been received by the deadline. The Secretary to the Cabinet then announced that Hichilema’s inauguration would proceed on 1 September, citing that same claim.
This is worth pausing on, because it is not the same story as an election being rigged. The government never had to win an argument about the vote count. It only had to keep the question of whether a petition existed unresolved for as long as the Constitution’s window allowed. It then declared that no petition existed, even though its own Chief Justice had said otherwise days earlier. Human Rights Watch called the closures a direct denial of access to justice. Zambia’s Chapter One Foundation has since petitioned the Constitutional Court to declare the shutdown itself unlawful, a case the judiciary has yet to determine.
That distinction matters more than it might look. An election stolen at the ballot box is a familiar kind of theft, and African courts, however imperfectly, have a template for adjudicating it. deduped_items.title: Can cloud seeding help end droughts in Africa?
deduped_items.summary: Cloud seeding promises to squeeze more rain from clouds in a world facing worsening water shortages. But the science remains uncertain, the costs are high and the risks are not fully understood. As droughts intensify across Africa, can a decades-old technology really help solve the continent’s water crisis?
deduped_items.body_text:
In the skies above Béni Mellal, on the edge of Morocco’s Middle Atlas, a Royal Gendarmerie Alpha Jet flies over a cloud identified several hours earlier. On the ground, a technician has treated the cloud base with smoke. At the signal, the pilot releases silver iodide into it to trigger rainfall. Science fiction? No – cloud seeding has been practised for decades in Morocco, as well as in around 50 countries worldwide, according to the World Meteorological Organisation.

deduped_items.title: نيبال: حين يتحول نجاح حماية الحياة البرية إلى تهديد لحياة السكان
deduped_items.summary: خلال نصف قرن، استطاعت نيبال أن تفرض نفسها كمرجع عالمي في مجال الحفاظ على البيئة. إذ تم تصنيف نحو 20٪ من أراضي هذا البلد الصغير الواقع في جبال الهيمالايا كمناطق محمية، نتيجة لسياسات مكافحة الصيد الجائر. وقد تم إنقاذ أنواع رمزية مثل وحيد القرن، التي كانت مهددة بالانقراض. لكن، وبشكل مفارِق، أدى هذا النجاح إلى زيادة الصراعات بين الحيوانات البرية والسكان المحليين الذين يعيشون على أطراف هذه المحميات الطبيعية. فكلما زاد عدد الحيوانات البرية، زادت حاجتها إلى توسيع نطاقها الطبيعي.

deduped_items.summary: خلال نصف قرن، استطاعت نيبال أن تفرض نفسها كمرجع عالمي في مجال الحفاظ على البيئة. إذ تم تصنيف نحو 20٪ من أراضي هذا البلد الصغير الواقع في جبال الهيمالايا كمناطق محمية، نتيجة لسياسات مكافحة الصيد الجائر. وقد تم إنقاذ أنواع رمزية مثل وحيد القرن، التي كانت مهددة بالانقراض. لكن، وبشكل مفارِق، أدى هذا النجاح إلى زيادة الصراعات بين الحيوانات البرية والسكان المحليين الذين يعيشون على أطراف هذه المحميات الطبيعية. فكلما زاد عدد الحيوانات البرية، زادت حاجتها إلى توسيع نطاقها الطبيعي.

deduped_items.summary: As the international community marks World Porridge Day on 10 October, the story of a young Malawian woman whose life was transformed by a daily school meal offers a reflection on the importance of school feeding programmes in the fight against hunger. Through the documentary Lettie, Mary's Meals revisits a story first told more than a decade ago, tracing one woman's journey from childhood hunger to hope. Read all
